title: DHS warns of threats to election posed by artificial intelligence
text:
DHS warns of threats to election posed by artificial intelligence
"This is a problem of today," one expert said.
The threat posed by artificial intelligence programs is real and creates a serious challenge going into the 2024 election, according to a new federal assessment.
The analysis, compiled by the Department of Homeland Security and obtained by ABC News, outlines how, with less than six months before Election Day, next-generation technologies meant to fuel advancement also offer opportunities for misuse that could threaten the democratic system's bedrock of elections.
"As the 2024 election cycle progresses, generative AI tools likely provide both domestic and foreign threat actors with enhanced opportunities for interference by aggravating emergent events, disrupting election processes, or attacking election infrastructure," the May 17 document said. Those tools, the bulletin said, can be wielded to "influence and sow discord" in upcoming U.S. elections by those who view them as "attractive" and "priority" targets.
"This is not a problem for the future. This is a problem of today," said John Cohen, the former intelligence chief at the Department of Homeland Security, and now an ABC News contributor. "Foreign and domestic threat actors have fully embraced the internet, and they are increasingly using advanced computing capabilities like artificial intelligence to conduct their illegal operations."
Already, those attempting to target elections have done so "by conducting cyber-enabled hack-and-leak campaigns, voice spoofing, online disinformation campaigns, and threatening or plotting attacks against symbols of the US elections," the bulletin said.
And now, the analysis warns, the innovative abilities of generative AI can be used against future elections.Those tools can be exploited "to confuse or overwhelm voters and election staff to disrupt their duties" by creating or sharing "altered" or deepfaked pictures, videos or audio clips "regarding the details of Election Day, such as claiming that a polling station is closed or that polling times have changed, or to generate or promote other tailored false information online."
On the eve of the New Hampshire primary in January, a robocall seeming to impersonate the voice of President Joe Biden circulated, encouraging recipients of the call to "save your vote" for the November general election, rather than participate in the state's primary, according to audio obtained at the time by ABC News.
That "generative AI-created audio message" was specifically flagged in the DHS analysis, which also noted "the timing of election-specific AI-generated media can be just as critical as the content itself, as it may take time to counter-message or debunk the false content permeating online."
"This may be one of the most difficult elections for Americans to navigate finding ground truth in our lifetimes," said Elizabeth Neumann, a DHS assistant secretary during the first years of Donald Trump's presidency, and now an ABC News contributor. "It's not just whether a politician is telling you the truth, but you won't even be able to trust your own eyes at the images you're seeing in your social media feeds, in your email and possibly even traditional media, if they don't do a good enough job vetting the material."
The 2024 race has been marked by increasingly toxic rhetoric, and the intermingling of inflammatory campaign trail hyperbole and courtroom theatrics, as Trump faces four criminal cases in which he maintains his innocence. Hate speech, misinformation and disinformation are running rampant on social media and in real life -- even as rapidly evolving technology remains vulnerable, experts said. Meanwhile, wars in the Middle East and Ukraine continue overseas, dividing Americans' views on foreign policy, with the conflicts rippling out in protests at major U.S. college campuses from coast to coast.
"Threat actors can attempt to exploit deepfake videos, audio content, or other generative AI media to amplify discontent," the DHS analysis said. "A well-timed deepfake or piece of AI-generated media for a targeted audience could spur individuals to take action that may result in violence or physical disruptions directed toward the elections or candidates."
The threat landscape has grown "more diverse and more complex," and protecting the integrity of U.S. elections faces more challenges than ever due to the accelerating sophistication of artificial intelligence, top intelligence officials told lawmakers last Wednesday.
"Using every tool we have is critical as the challenge is expanding," Director of National Intelligence Avril Haines told a Senate committee holding a hearing focused on threats to the 2024 elections. "There are an increasing number of foreign actors, including non-state entities who are looking to engage in election influence activities," she said, adding "relevant emerging technologies, particularly generative AI and big data analytics, are increasing the threat by enabling the proliferation of influence actors who can conduct targeted campaigns."
"Innovations in AI have enabled foreign influence actors to produce seemingly authentic and tailored messaging more efficiently, at greater scale," Haines added. "Even as the threat landscape is becoming increasingly complicated, it is my view that the U.S. government has never been better prepared to address the challenge," in part thanks to lessons learned from the 2016 presidential election.
Authorities at every level need to be ready to defend against artificial intelligence disseminating fake news at this delicate moment, experts said.
"One of the most important things we need to be doing now is educating and preparing the public. Because they will be the people who are being targeted with this content -- the public is the intended target -- and the objective is to influence how people behave," Cohen said.
"State and local officials need to have a plan, so that when this content is detected, they can use trusted sources of communication to counteract and correct inaccurate information. Once that content hits, it's going to spread across the online media ecosystem rapidly, and has to be counteracted immediately," Cohen added. "Law enforcement and our security community have been slow to adapt to this rapidly evolving threat environment. We're still using the strategies of yesterday to deal with a threat of today. In a way, it's bringing a knife to a gunfight."

title: ‘I Want That Sweet Baby’: AI-Generated Kids Draw Predators On TikTok And Instagram
text:
Images of AI children on TikTok and Instagram are becoming magnets for many with a sexual interest in minors. But when this content is legal and depicts fake people, it falls into a messy, troubling gray area.
By Alexandra S. Levine, Forbes Staff
The following article contains discussions of disturbing social media content.
The girls in the photos on TikTok and Instagram look like they could be five or six years old. On the older end, not quite thirteen.
They’re pictured in lace and leather, bikinis and crop tops. They’re dressed suggestively as nurses, superheroes, ballerinas and french maids. Some wear bunny ears or devil horns; others, pigtails and oversized glasses. They’re black, white and Asian, blondes, redheads and brunettes. They were all made with AI, and they’ve become magnets for the attention of a troubling audience on some of the biggest social media apps in the world—older men.
“AI makes great works of art: I would like to have a pretty little virgin like that in my hands to make it mine,” one TikTok user commented on a recent post of young blonde girls in maid outfits, with bows around their necks and flowers in their hair.
“If this is AI-generated, does it make me bad to say she’s hot as everything put together?” another TikToker wrote on a slideshow of fully clothed little girls in Spider-Man costumes. “She’s not real, but I’ve got a great imagination.”
“It shouldn’t be wrong either way,” replied another, whose username contained “p3do,” which can be algospeak, or coded language, for “pedo.”
“You can’t violate her because it’s an AI image,” said one more.
Similar remarks flooded photos of AI kids on Instagram. “I would love to take her innocence even if she’s a fake image,” one person wrote on a post of a small, pale child dressed as a bride. On another, of a young girl in short-shorts, the same user commented on “her cute pair of small size [breasts],” depicted as two apple emojis, “and her perfect innocent slice of cherry pie down below.” And on a picture of a pre-teen in spaghetti straps, someone named “Gary” said: “Nice little buds. When she gets older they’ll be good sized melons.”
“Looks tasty.” “Do you do home delivery?” “The perfect age to be taken advantage of.” “I want that sweet baby.” “Can you do a test where she jumps out of my phone into my bed?” said others on TikTok and Instagram. Forbes found hundreds of posts and comments like these on images of AI-generated kids on the platforms from 2024 alone. Many were tagged to musical hits—like Beyonce’s “Texas Hold ‘Em,” Taylor Swift’s “Shake It Off” and Tracy Chapman’s “Fast Car”—to help them reach more eyeballs.
Child predators have prowled most every major social media app—where they can hide behind screens and anonymous usernames—but TikTok and Instagram’s popularity with teens and minors has made them both top destinations. And though platforms’ struggle to crack down on child sexual abuse material (or CSAM) predates today’s AI boom, AI text-to-image generators are making it even easier for predators to find or create exactly what they’re looking for.
The tools have driven a surge of AI-generated CSAM, which is illegal even if it’s fake. But the images uncovered in the reporting of this story fall into a gray area. They’re not explicit, but they are sexualized. They feature minors, but not real ones. They appear to be legal, yet the comments made on them suggest dangerous intent. Child safety and forensics experts have described them as portals to far darker, and potentially criminal, activity. That raises questions across tech and law enforcement about how a scourge of suggestive, fake images of kids that don’t exist should be dealt with—or whether, if they’re not explicit and legal, it should be addressed at all.
Tech companies are required, under federal law, to report suspected CSAM and child sexual exploitation on their platforms to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, a nonprofit that funnels information about that illegal activity to law enforcement. But they are not obligated to flag or remove images like those described in this story. Still, NCMEC told Forbes it believes social media companies should take them down—even if they’re legal.
“These are all being trained off of images of real children, whether depicted in full likeness or not, so NCMEC doesn't really see that side of the argument that there's a world where this is okay,” said Fallon McNulty, director of the organization’s CyberTipline, its reporting hub for tech companies. A recent study by the Stanford Internet Observatory found that one of the most popular text-to-image generative AI tools on the market today, Stable Diffusion 1.5, had been trained on CSAM, of real kids, scraped from across the web.
“Especially given some of the commentaries that the images are attracting, it doesn't sound like the audience that is reviewing, ingesting, consuming those images is innocent,” McNulty added. “I would hope to see that they're removing that content and not creating a space on their platforms for individuals to be sexualizing children.”
The images of AI-generated kids were tagged to hits from Taylor Swift, Beyonce and Tracy Chapman to help them reach more eyeballs.
TikTok and Instagram permanently removed the accounts, videos and comments referenced in this story after Forbes asked about them; both companies said they violated platform rules.
“TikTok has strict policies against AI-generated content of minors to protect young people and keep TikTok inhospitable to behavior that seeks to harm them,” said spokesperson Jamie Favazza. On Friday, the company instituted a new synthetic media policy prohibiting such content if it contains the likeness of anyone under 18, and it takes down posts that break its rules, regardless of whether they were altered with AI.
Sophie Vogel, a spokesperson for Instagram’s parent company Meta, said the company does not allow, and removes, real and AI-generated material that sexualizes or exploits children. In cases where the content appears to be benign, they still remove accounts, profiles or Pages dedicated to sharing images of children or commenting on their appearance, Vogel said. Both TikTok and Meta report AI-generated CSAM they find on their platforms to NCMEC.
A ‘Gateway’ To Illegal Content
One popular creator of AI-generated kids had 80,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram, a number that climbed by the thousands as Forbes was reporting this story. The account’s bio, written in Mandarin, said “Woman With Chopsticks.” Forbes was unable to determine who was running it, but its most viral posts were viewed nearly half a million times, liked more than 10,000 times, saved or shared thousands of times, and drew hundreds of comments.
Many of its followers—based on their profile photos, names or handles, bios and comments—appeared to be older men.
Digital forensics expert Heather Mahalik Barnhart said that in her past work on these “child erotica” cases, the followers often offered clear clues that could point investigators toward potential predators. “Child erotica is the gateway,” she told Forbes, and “when you look at who’s following it, it’s not normal.”
These types of accounts also do more to expose potential offenders because they’re emboldened out in the open. “People feel more secure because it’s not fully exposed children, therefore not CSAM,” said Mahalik, who leads software company Cellebrite’s work helping NCMEC and law enforcement use its tech in child exploitation investigations. She noted it’s imperative that law enforcement more closely examine who follows these accounts and look for a pattern of behavior.
The TikTok account shared an instructional video showing followers how to generate and perfect their own photos of young girls, down to the girls’ teeth.
“Even though I am many years older than you, as soon as I saw your eyes I fell in love with you,” said one commenter on the TikTok account, who was following other handles featuring even more suggestive images of children. (Another frequent commenter, who made remarks like “open wide,” was running an account with posts of real girls doing splits and stretching in leotards.)
Some commenters on the TikTok and Instagram posts from “Woman With Chopsticks” asked what AI model was used to make the AI children, suggesting they could be interested in producing more. (“This stuff is amazing, I wish could find an app that could create this,” one man wrote a week ago on an Instagram of a scantily clad young blonde in a bralette.) In January, the TikTok account shared a three-minute instructional video showing followers how to generate and perfect their own photos of young girls, down to the girls’ teeth.
Other commenters didn’t seem to know the images were fake; though the creator labeled some of the posts “AI-generated,” as TikTok requires, it can be difficult for the naked eye to tell they’re not real, which also makes it harder for law enforcement to pinpoint actual victims. (Meta is building tools that will be able to identify images made using OpenAI, Midjourney, Microsoft, Google, Adobe, and Shutterstock and will then begin labeling AI-generated content posted to Facebook, Instagram and Threads, according to Vogel, the Meta spokesperson.)
Lloyd Richardson, director of IT at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, said that regardless of whether these borderline images are AI or real, they’re a “gateway” to more severe or illegal content, often on other platforms, which then poses “a clear safety risk to children.”
“The underlying issue is that this subset of images leads to networking opportunities for offenders,” Richardson told Forbes, noting that they’ll often move their conversations to private direct messages. “These images can act as signposts for promoting links toward CSAM in other channels.”
A January 13 slideshow on TikTok of little girls in silk pajamas showed this type of back-and-forth in action. “This works for me,” one person wrote in the comments, to which another replied: “I just messaged you.”
“This is why companies cannot simply moderate content in isolation by looking at images alone,” Richardson added. “They have to be taken into the broader context of how they are being shared, viewed and followed. This is of course more challenging as it can require contextual assessment which can require human moderation staff.” (Favazza, the TikTok spokesperson, said they use automation to help flag possible evidence of predatory behavior.)
Got a tip about TikTok, Instagram, or children’s safety issues on social media? Reach out securely to Alexandra S. Levine on Signal/WhatsApp at (310) 526–1242 or email at alevine@forbes.com.
TikTok’s powerful algorithm also makes it easier for those with a sexual interest in children to find even more of these kinds of images. As Forbes was reporting this story, TikTok began recommending additional prompts—like “ai generated boys” and “ai fantasy girl.” And TikTok’s “For You” feed, where users land when they open the app and that serves up viral videos TikTok thinks they’ll like, ensures that they reach even more of TikTok’s 1 billion users.
McNulty, from NCMEC, said one of the greatest risks of AI kids having these viral moments on social media, even if the images are noncriminal, is that people can become desensitized to how dangerous they can be.
“As a society,” she said, “are we just gonna get used to this type of content and say that's okay?”

title: Why Ubisoft And Other Studios Are Doubling-Down On Web3 And AI Gaming
text:
CoinGecko recently shared that 29 of the world’s 40 biggest game studios are investing in Web3 gaming, with 7 actively developing their own Web3 games in-house. This doesn’t surprise me one bit - it’s been clear for some time that research, development, talent, and investment have been pouring into the GameFi space. Game7’s State of Web Gaming report at the end of last year suggested that at least $15 billion of institutional investment has moved into blockchain gaming since 2018. Now we’re seeing the output.
There are so many reasons to be optimistic about this nascent space, especially when you see all of the incredible global gaming events paying attention to Web3, useful innovations that will accelerate player experience (such as portable Web3 identities), and huge announcements being made every week. We’re entering a golden era for Web3 gaming, and I’ll tell you why.
Major Games Expositions
The Games Developers Conference, or GDC 2024, was the biggest Web3 gaming event of the year so far, took place in March in San Francisco. With over 30,000 attendees, hundreds of speakers, sponsors, and investors present, it was the who’s who of GameFi, and that made it the perfect opportunity for new games to demo and existing games to grow support.
Next on the calendar is the inaugural Decentraland
I’ve seen other projects try to do this kind of online event, to mixed reviews, but I feel confident that Decentraland can pull off this ambitious event, draw a big crowd, line up some impressive panels, and stream the whole thing without a hitch. From what I’ve seen, there will be some big prizes up for grabs for the best new Web3 games, which is a great incentive to get studios to show what they’re working on.
Epic Game Launches & Announcements in Q1 2024
The start of this year has been some massive announcements, launches, beta tests, and teasers. It’s hard to keep track of it all. I’ve got my eye on a few titles, like MetalCore, which is in its second Beta test right now and recently announced an enormous partnership deal with Pixelmon which will see a crossover of more than one million players. Then there’s Star Atlas, which has been in development and building hype for several years and is Solana’s flagship Web3 game - reportedly accounting for around 8% of all SOL
One game that performed well over the last few years was My Neighbor Alice, winning several awards and growing a solid user base. Now, I see that their development team is building a GenAI game called Cloudborn, complete with an AI-NPC companion, AI-generated environments, and NFT
The game looks a bit further behind in development than some others, but at least it’s not facing a legal battle, like Shrapnel. While it could potentially be the most groundbreaking Web3 game of the year, Shrapnel has announced internal issues that are slowing down their development, despite being in the pre-alpha stage.
One more game I want to mention is Off The Grid, which will be available on PC, Xbox, and PlayStation 5. Finally, AAA Web3 titles are finding their way onto consoles. This is going to be a great way of onboarding traditional gamers into this new space, without forcing them away from their preferred platform.
Ubisoft Returns to Web3 Gaming With AI
I mentioned that only 7 of the world's top 40 gaming studios are building Web3 games in house. The list is Take-Two Interactive, Nexon, Bandai Namco, Konami Holdings, Krafton, Square Enix, and Ubisoft. However, it’s Ubisoft that I’m most interested in right now.
Nicolas Pouard, Vice President of the Ubisoft Strategic Innovation Lab, and the Head of Blockchain Initiatives at Ubisoft Entrepreneurs Lab recently shared that Ubisoft’s Web3 games are approaching completion and should be ready to launch this year. This is not Ubisoft’s first foray into Web3 gaming, after their Quartz blockchain gaming initiative with Ghost Recon: Breakpoint in 2021. That project saw a lot of fan backlash over NFT integration, which saw Ubisoft eventually decide to make unique Web3 experiences instead of trying to impose a Web3 layer onto their popular existing Web2 titles and loyal audience.
In an interview with VentureBeat, Pouard revealed that they are working closely with a community of Web3-interested gamers to get things right, and that in 2021, the technology wasn’t mature enough. In 2024, I expect them to strike gold.
And the integration of AI into Web3 gaming is revolutionizing how games are developed, played, and experienced. I’ve been working in AI since 2013 and I know personally how AI enhances the immersive qualities of games by creating more realistic and responsive environments, as well as intelligent NPCs that adapt to player actions in real time.
This not only enriches the gameplay but also ensures that each gaming session is unique and engaging. Ubisoft, for instance, is leveraging AI to develop dynamic game worlds and complex character behaviors that evolve based on player interactions. This approach provides a deeply personalized gaming experience that goes beyond traditional static gameplay, setting new standards for player engagement.
Leading the charge alongside Ubisoft, other top companies like Animoca Brands and Dapper Labs are also at the forefront of integrating AI and Web3 technologies into their gaming ecosystems.
Animoca Brands is utilizing AI to enhance its blockchain-based games by enabling sophisticated game mechanics and player-driven economies, allowing players to truly own and monetize their in-game assets. I was chatting with Yat Siu, Co-founder and Executive Chairman, Animoca Brands, and he shared with me that "At Animoca Brands, we believe that the power of Web3 gaming lies in its ability to revolutionize the way players interact with and own digital assets. Web3 technology empowers players with true ownership, allowing them to trade, monetize, and truly benefit from their in-game achievements and assets in a decentralized ecosystem.”
And he continued telling me that “adding AI to this mix is like giving our games a superpower. AI enhances the gaming experience by creating dynamic, responsive environments and intelligent NPCs that adapt to each player's unique style and decisions. This combination of Web3 and AI not only elevates player engagement but also opens up new realms of creativity and personalization, making each gaming experience unique and deeply immersive."
Dapper Labs, known for its NBA Top Shot platform, is using AI to provide personalized experiences and predictive analytics, ensuring that players are always presented with content that is most relevant to their preferences. These companies exemplify how AI, when combined with the decentralized principles of Web3, is transforming the gaming industry, offering unprecedented levels of interactivity, ownership, and personalization.
The Death of “Web3 Gaming”
Web3 Gaming is going to die in the next few years. I mean the term, “Web3 Gaming”, because I am absolutely confident that every game studio out there will eventually use Web3 in their development and at that point the term becomes meaningless. It will just become “Gaming”. I’m looking forward to that. I’ve heard a similar sentiment from Skale’s CEO, Jack O’Holleran, who said “We will all be so successful at integrating the value propositions of blockchain into games that every game in the world will start leveraging this far better”.
Web3 Gaming is dead. Long live Web3 Gaming!
I had a great conversation with the Earn Alliance CEO and founder Joseph “Coop” Cooper. He told me that “Many of us are working toward a day when web3 gaming is just referred to as gaming. My hope (or estimate) is that we’ve achieved this by 2026. To get there, we need really great games built on blockchain that people just love to play, period. With Earn Alliance, we’re focused on solving the problem of discoverability by creating a unified hub that makes finding and playing all of the web3 games out there easy, fun, and rewarding. This dedication to creating opportunities for gamers is very dear to us, as we recognize that the web3 game industry is just beginning – involving highly experimental tokenomics and entrepreneurs exploring the challenge of building network effects. The next step is mass adoption by lessening the friction of utilizing crypto assets for gamers.”
As we continued to talk, “As part of this, we’ve introduced the web3 stealth zombie battle royale game Last Remains, which is our take on what an innovative game can do with blockchain technology. We believe the industry needs more players taking risks and incorporating the best of web2 game design with the open economy of the web3 world. As part of this strategy, we’re committed that 50% of net profit is being reinvested into competitive prize pools.”
“The future of gaming lies in the seamless integration of blockchain technology, making games more accessible and enjoyable for everyone. By creating tools for gamers, building fan bases, and ensuring easy utilization of these tools, we pave the way for all consumers to engage in the new era, regardless of what terminology people use to describe it.”
Final Thoughts on Web3’s Ascension
Up and up we go. More players, more development, and more innovation. It’s remarkable what time, investment, and talent can do when combined and applied to a well-defined mission. Just look at the Ubisoft example I mentioned. NFTs were novel and scary in 2021, now they’re part of popular culture. Gamers are coming around to the benefits of Web3, for the greater good.

title: Council Post: What To Know About Using A GenAI Co-Marketer
text:
Pratik is the CEO North America at Netcore Cloud and Netcore Unbxd.
The digital marketing landscape is undergoing a tectonic shift. For the past several years, marketers have been using AI and machine learning to automate tasks and improve efficiency (e.g., content creation, customer segmentation, etc.). Now, marketers have access to technology that can elevate conversion effectiveness.
In fact, Forrester Research recently proclaimed that “over the next decade, generative AI will be the fulcrum that accelerates growth: It will be the pivot point upon which business growth rises.”
I’ve witnessed (and participated in) this shift for the past decade as a marketing technology product leader and now as the CEO of a company focused on generative AI (GenAI). Having personally designed and developed technology to drive marketer efficiency, I am incredibly excited about the waves of change.
The Application Space
GenAI is forcing CMOs to reevaluate their marketing roadmaps and add flexibility to incorporate GenAI in future plans. In fact, according to Gartner in August 2023, "63% of marketing leaders are planning to invest in generative AI in the next 24 months."
Here are five key areas where GenAI could transform marketing.
1. Workflow Optimization
The faster marketers can act on customer insights, the better their chance of engaging with their audiences. GenAI can help marketers drive internal velocity through better:
• Segmentation: Grouping customers based on demographics, interests or purchase history. It allows targeted content delivery to broader segments (e.g., location-based product recommendations).
• Content Creation: Generating product descriptions, blog posts aligned with customer behavior and personalized social media captions.
• Channel Orchestration: Scheduling personalized communication, utilizing chatbots for recommendations and serving targeted ads across platforms.
2. The AI Co-Marketer
GenAI can serve as a marketing assistant by offering insights into audience preferences. By dynamically adapting marketing strategies in real time and providing suggestions for improvements based on performance metrics, GenAI co-marketers can optimize marketing efforts.
GenAI can also predict the next best action (NBA) for individual customers, leading to more personalized experiences, upgrading from a current state of marketing campaigns for everyone in segments to a future state of goal-based personalization activation.
3. Advanced Customer Understanding
Until recently, marketers relied on optimization testing to develop an understanding of audiences. To achieve statistically significant results, many optimization programs needed to run for extended periods to generate the requisite data.
Today, GenAI can accelerate the path from insight to action by analyzing not only browsing behavior and channel engagements but also customer reviews, social media interactions and intent both on-brand and off-brand to:
• Uncover emotions, motivations and pain points.
• Predict customer preferences and future needs.
• Develop a comprehensive understanding of each customer.
4. Multi-Channel Analysis And Real-Time Feedback
Even if your brand currently holds a significant place in customers' lives, failing to meet their expectations can quickly lead them to turn to a competitor.
As digital interactions increasingly dominate customer engagement, both the digital experiences customers have—and the data companies collect from them—will evolve, presenting both challenges and opportunities. GenAI can help by:
• Analyzing customer interactions across various channels in real time.
• Identifying customer intent and engagement based on click-through rates and dwell time.
• Refining predictions continuously through real-time feedback loops.
5. AI-Powered Scenario Simulation
AI can assist marketers in achieving their goals by building predictive models that simulate the outcomes of various marketing strategies.
It can analyze historical and real-time data to project the potential impacts of different actions and evaluate the results of these simulations, providing marketers with insights into possible adjustments and allowing them to refine their strategies by:
• Answering questions like, "How do I generate 3% more conversions today?" Marketers will need to provide scenarios that start with a goal (like revenue) and constraints (like profitability), and AI can guide a marketing roadmap set of actions to address that need.
• Simulating the effectiveness of personalized messages and content formats.
• Predicting the potential impact of different offers on customer behavior and conversion rates.
• Identifying the action with the highest probability of achieving the desired outcome.
Human-Augmented AI
While GenAI is powerful, human intervention remains crucial. Machines are well equipped to handle automated tasks and repetitive functions to assist marketers and make them more productive, but strategic guidance is still required.
In fact, Gartner forecasts that “by 2025, organizations that use AI in the marketing function will shift 75% of their staff’s operations from production to more strategic activities.” These activities will certainly include AI prompt engineering to get the most valid results from their AI technology, but will also incorporate:
• Predicting Customer Response: Marketing specialists can leverage industry knowledge to refine segmentation criteria GenAI uses for improved accuracy.
• Identifying Purchase-Ready Customers: Human oversight ensures data accuracy and incorporates business rules for refined targeting.
• Fine-Tuning Customer Segmentation: Marketers can manually review high-risk segments and personalize interventions based on the specific customer situation.
• Creative Direction And Brand Voice: Human copywriters can refine AI-generated content to ensure it aligns with the brand's messaging and resonates with the target audience.
• Emotional Intelligence: Marketers can add elements of humor, empathy or storytelling to connect with customers on an emotional level.
• Strategic Planning And Channel Selection: Humans develop the overall marketing strategy and determine the appropriate channels for reaching specific segments. GenAI personalizes messaging and timing within those channels.
• Channel-Specific Optimization: Marketers leverage their understanding of specific channels (email, social media) to optimize content and CTAs further.
• A/B Testing And Continuous Improvement: Marketers can provide human-in-the-loop A/B testing, which is essential to evaluate and refine GenAI outputs through testing different content variations and channel combinations.
The Path Ahead
GenAI is revolutionizing marketing by enabling hyper-personalization and predictive capabilities. We are well on the way to a goal-driven, campaignless future that supercharges personalization to the proverbial segment of one.
However, human expertise remains vital for strategic planning, creative direction and emotional intelligence. By combining the power of GenAI with human ingenuity, marketers can craft exceptional customer experiences and propel their brands toward a future of unprecedented growth and engagement.

title: Council Post: The Need For AI-Informed Defense: How AI Empowers Security Teams
text:
Joe Ariganello is the VP of Product Marketing at MixMode, where he works with cutting-edge AI technology.
As a cybersecurity product marketer, I know firsthand how words can impact a product's perception. In the past, I've gone against my better judgement and spent time developing materials trying to convince a market that a product was something it wasn't, despite my objections and recommendations against doing so.
Now that I've learned better and have progressed in my career, I find myself at the center of the artificial intelligence revolution in cybersecurity, trying to navigate the perception of AI within it and how CISOs and security teams have been previously burned by false promises.
The Evolution Of AI
AI has undergone a significant transformation over the years in cybersecurity. In 2013, DARPA generated three different waves of AI. Understanding them might alleviate some concerns about utilizing AI in cybersecurity.
1. Prevention (Legacy, Rules-Based): This initial wave focused on using AI to build better prevention methods. Security professionals defined specific rules and criteria for identifying malicious activity. AI then screened data against these predefined rules, flagging anything suspicious for further investigation. While effective for known threats, this approach struggled to adapt to constantly evolving cyberattacks.
2. Detection And Response (Machine Learning): The second wave introduced machine learning (ML). Unlike pre-defined rules, ML algorithms learn and adapt over time. Security teams fed them vast amounts of data, including past security incidents and known malware samples. The ML models identified patterns and anomalies, detecting novel threats and suspicious activity that might have bypassed rule-based systems. This wave significantly improved threat detection but relied on human analysts to investigate and respond.
3. Real-Time Detection, Prediction And Prevention (Generative AI): The latest wave of AI in cybersecurity utilizes generative AI, which can analyze data to create realistic simulations of cyberattacks. This empowers security teams with three key advantages: proactively luring attackers with fake systems (honeypots), predicting potential attacks based on past data, and even taking automated actions to contain threats like isolating infected systems. This signifies a shift from simply reacting to threats to proactively anticipating and preventing them.
As AI technology continues to develop, providers are pioneering even more sophisticated applications, such as:
• Self-Supervised Learning AI: Some AI models can learn from data and continuously improve their algorithms, adapting to new threats without human intervention.
• Explainable AI: Develop AI that can detect threats and explain its reasoning to security analysts, fostering better collaboration and trust between humans and AI.
Overcoming The Past
CISOs and security teams have been burned by AI in the past, leading to some skepticism about its current iteration. Past issues with AI in cybersecurity include:
• False Positives And Negatives: These systems often generated a high volume of false positives (flagging harmless activity as threats) and negatives (missing genuine threats). This wasted valuable analyst time and created a sense of unreliability.
• Data Dependency And Bias: The effectiveness of past AI hinged on the quality and quantity of training data. Biases within the data could lead the AI to prioritize specific threats over others, creating blind spots.
• The "Black Box" Problem: Early AI often functioned as a "black box," making it difficult to understand how it arrived at its conclusions. This lack of transparency made it hard to trust its recommendations.
Why Today's Evolution Is Different
The challenge is getting security professionals to understand how and why this evolution differs. Start with the following:
• Focus On Accuracy: Modern AI development prioritizes reducing false positives and negatives. Techniques like anomaly detection and threat scoring help identify genuine threats more accurately.
• Emphasis On Explainability: There's a growing focus on explainable AI (XAI). This allows security teams to understand the reasoning behind the AI's recommendations, fostering trust and enabling informed decision-making.
• Human-AI Collaboration: The current approach views AI as a powerful tool to augment human analysts, not replace them. Security teams leverage AI's processing power for threat detection and prioritization while reserving critical judgment and decision-making for human expertise.
While past experiences with AI were frustrating, the current evolution offers a more robust and trustworthy solution. With continuous improvement in AI's capabilities and a focus on human-AI collaboration, the future of cybersecurity looks far brighter.
An AI-Informed Defense: How Security Teams And AI Can Work Together
By leveraging AI's analytical prowess and applying it to defense, security teams can gain a significant edge in threat detection, response and overall security posture to form an AI-informed defense, which includes:
• Enhanced Threat Detection: AI can continuously analyze vast amounts of data from network traffic, user activity, and endpoint devices. This allows them to identify subtle anomalies that might escape human analysts, detecting potential threats in real time.
• Improved Threat Analysis And Prioritization: AI can analyze past security incidents and threat intelligence feeds to identify patterns and predict future attacks. This allows security teams to prioritize threats based on potential severity and allocate resources effectively.
• Security Automation: AI can automate routine tasks such as log analysis, vulnerability scanning and patch management. This frees security personnel to focus on higher-level tasks and strategic security planning.
Building A Successful AI-Informed Defense
While AI offers significant advantages, it's important to remember that it's a tool, not a silver bullet. Security teams remain vital—ensuring data quality, interpreting AI insights and making key decisions.
This ongoing collaboration is crucial for security teams and AI to form a powerful defense against cyber threats by working together.
This ever-evolving threat landscape demands a dynamic defense strategy. The current third wave of AI can deliver it.

title: Finding A Home For AI In The K-12 Curriculum
text:
“For the past 100 years, we have emphasized fundamental skills such as math, reading, and writing in schools, recognizing their importance in preparing young students to become productive, successful adults who contribute to society. Given the current societal and workplace changes, we should now include AI literacy in this list.”—Bill Salak.
The challenge is determining where and how AI should be situated within the broader curricular arc. To do so we must carefully consider the type of tool AI is and the desired benefits that would come from its use. This article comes from a recent conversation with Bill Salak, CTO/COO of Brainly, whose AI Learning Companion is used by 15 million students each day.
What Kind Of Tool Is AI?
AI is undoubtedly a tool capable of skillful and unskilled use. But what kind of tool is it? Is it like keyboarding, an instrumental tool introduced intentionally at a particular moment and then refined through incidental use in later courses? Or is it more a foundational skill, like reading, that effectively rewires the brain, reshaping the rest of one’s educational experience?
Some tools change the nature of what is taught and how things are taught. Prior to publishing, lecturing was essentially a reading out of books that students then needed to copy down on paper. Once students could get copies of books from printers, the way that lectures were use changed substantially. Similarly, graphing calculators altered the nature of mathematics instruction because it enabled students to move from wrestling with equations to see what they looked like to having near-immediate gratification going through an involved graphing process. Does generative AI mark a similar shift, providing students with an automated way to experiment with thesis statements and supports to see what the resulting essay might look like without going through an involved process of actually writing it?
Attending To The Process And Not Just The Results
The ubiquity of mathematics as a required topic in high schools is not in the service of developing mathematicians. Instead, it serves three purposes. First, basic numeracy is as important as basic literacy for getting around the world. The second is that a facility with basic mathematics is essential for developing a facility with basic science—mathematics is the “language of science,” as it is often called. The third is that learning how to do mathematics develops critical faculties that make working with information easier. It may be that learning to use AI is similar. In a world where AI abounds, it becomes an essential skill. Where the ability to quickly generate and consumer semi-polished output is expected, having a basic command of AI as a tool becomes necessary. Finally, it may be that repeated use of AI in different controlled ways develops broader cognitive capabilities for dealing with information critically.
Show Your Prompts
In education, "show your work" has long been the cry of mathematics teachers. This is because what is being taught is not the ability to produce solutions to problems but the process of information manipulation that leads to answers.
The challenge is that proper evaluation of work requires understanding the process that leads to the answer and not just the answer itself. In the case of AI, the cry may evolve to "show your prompts." I am less interested in the particulars you are creating and more interested in the process you are using to create them. If you get the wrong answer to a problem, I can only say that you are wrong. If I can see the process you used that led to the wrong answer, then I can take active measures to guide your learning.
Moving beyond “show your prompts” is adopting an agentic approach to using AI. Rather than treating it as a black box to which a student hands a question, it becomes an assistant to which instructions are given and where intermediate results are expected. By refining the ability to instruct the AI, one improves the results that the AI can produce. In this way, interactive learning still leads to better results. Still, rather than the results reflecting the student doing the computations, they reflect the student using the tool that does the computations. In this way, the use of AI is not fundamentally different from the use of a spreadsheet to perform a complex set of mathematical calculations.
When AI Becomes Willful
One of the problems with generative AI, when it arises to the level of an assistant, is that it can take on a personality of its own and make decisions that constrain the learning space.
Asking an AI like Gemini to solve a simple word problem can result in a lengthy discourse about the problem's inappropriateness and an outright refusal to do the work. Asking for answers to certain questions or illustrations about history can yield responses that are politically correct while not factually correct.
In such cases, AI is less like a tool, which can rightly be expected to reflect the will of its user, and more like a willful employee intentionally thwarting the boss's intent. While we seem to accept this behavior in an AI, we would never tolerate a word processor that, instead of just underlining misspellings and flagging grammatical errors, also performed various fact-checking services. This could range from the mundane, such as correcting a student's embellishment of their summer resume, to the pernicious, such as enforcing doctrinal correctness on students attending a religious school.
AI’s true threat to education becomes apparent when situations like this emerge. The problem is not that students will become lazy and unable to write for themselves. It is that they will become lazy and unable to think for themselves. When enforced conformity to the narrative replaces argumentation as the mode of persuasion, education gives way to indoctrination. At this moment, AI ceases to be a new tool for exploring ideas, and the ideal of Socrates with his students in the Agora seems far away.
And Yet AI Is Inescapable
If the goal of education is to prepare students for college and career, then regardless of how AI is introduced into the curriculum, it is essential for students to leave high school with a sufficient understanding of its utilities and sufficient knowledge of how to deploy it when appropriate. Viewed in this way, the question is less about whether AI should be introduced but rather what is the best strategy by which it can be introduced.
AI is more than just a tool; it is a new mode of information use that requires its own literacy. Integrating AI education into the curriculum is necessary to produce informed citizens able to navigate the complexities of the world and avail themselves of the opportunities found therein. As we continue to grapple with the ethical and practical implications of AI, it is crucial that we find the right place for it in our educational systems—a place that ensures competence without engendering dependence and that expands the horizons of thought rather than artificially constraining the discourse, and that allows AI to emerge as a tool of enlightenment.

title: Inside Quora’s Quest For Relevance: Why CEO Adam D’Angelo Has Gone All In On AI
text:
“Can I show you a demo?” Adam D’Angelo says as he prepares to share his screen on Zoom.
The CEO of Quora is extolling the virtues of Poe, the company’s platform for letting people chat with multiple AI models at a time. But during a test earlier that day for what should have been an easy task—generating a logo design using my name—the service had glitched. D’Angelo is quick to jump into troubleshoot mode. (I probably hadn’t set up Poe to access an image-generating model, he diagnoses.)
Last year, D’Angelo said at an AI event that most of the company’s energy these days is devoted to Poe, a service the company launched last year that serves as an interface for using and comparing multiple AI models, as well as bots built on top of them. That means less energy on Quora, the nearly 15-year-old Q&A forum that D’Angelo founded after leaving his post as Facebook’s CTO. But D’Angelo is so excited about AI’s potential that he’s gotten hands-on with the company’s new product, which has its own URL, separate from Quora.
“Poe needs more of my attention because it's in this more rapidly changing landscape,” D’Angelo told Forbes. “Quora has been around for many years now. It doesn't need to adapt. It doesn't need to change every week.” Quora’s goals are quarterly, he said, whereas Poe’s targets are set every two weeks.
The two products are vastly different. Quora is a message board where people answer questions like “What did Marilyn Monroe carry in her coffin?” and “What is the best small business to start in Gambia?” Meanwhile Poe, which stands for “Platform for Open Exploration,” is a freemium $200 per year subscription service that gives people access to several models, including OpenAI’s GPT-4, Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini. With the service, users can sample multiple models at once, comparing how each one tackles the same prompt. Developers can build bots on top of those models, creating, for example, an AI focused specifically on travel booking or creating coloring books for school children. Those developers can get paid per query, adding another revenue stream for people building AI tools. D’Angelo likens Poe to a web browser for AI, making the tech more accessible, like Netscape did three decades earlier.
“Poe needs more of my attention because it's in this more rapidly changing landscape.”
On its face, Poe and Quora don’t seem connected. But D’Angelo says Poe was born out of AI experiments the company began running two years ago, where it used OpenAI’s GPT-3 to generate answers for Quora questions. They were not as good as human-written answers, but the company found that there was a sweet spot for AI-generated answers: replies to niche questions that no human had ever written an answer for. Getting a lower quality AI answer was better than waiting around for a human to answer your question, he concluded. The experience resembled something more like private chat than an open forum, D’Angelo realized, so the company set out to build that kind of service.
D’Angelo’s rallying of the company around Poe comes at a confounding time for Quora. Founded in 2010, it has become a venerable throwback to the late web 2.0 era, surviving where rivals like Yahoo Answers fizzled out. But it hasn’t evolved into the modern era compared to competitors like Reddit, which went public in March and long ago became a cultural hub of the internet. That raises an interesting question: Who still uses Quora, really. It's hard to say, but the anecdotal evidence isn't great. Earlier this year, Slate proclaimed Quora dead. And on Quora itself, "Is quora dead" has been asked many times dating back to at least 2017. As one respondent answered, “Maybe Quora [has] just run its course, sort of like Yahoo or MySpace."
D’Angelo declined to comment on Quora’s revenue, though the company says it gets 400 million users a month.
With Poe, a seemingly disparate product from Quora, the company’s trajectory has gotten more murky. Is it a social forum backed by an advertising business model along the lines of Reddit, or is it going to become a player in AI? D’Angelo says it’s now poised for the latter. In January, the company announced $75 million in funding from Andreessen Horowitz to build out Poe.
“Maybe Quora just run its course, sort of like Yahoo or MySpace."
D’Angelo has had an inside look at the explosion in generative AI over the last few years in part because he’s been a board member at OpenAI since 2018, when it was still a nonprofit. But that also meant D’Angelo was at the center of the AI universe during one of the most dramatic boardroom power struggles in recent history. In November, the ChatGPT maker’s board fired CEO and founder Sam Altman, citing a lack of “candid” communication. The bombshell announcement set off a firestorm in Silicon Valley, and within five days, the board reversed course and rehired Altman. As part of the reinstatement, OpenAI replaced every board member except D’Angelo.
Poe does have some overlap with OpenAI’s GPT Store, a hub for customized AI bots that was announced less than two weeks before the ouster, leading to some speculation from industry observers about D’Angelo’s role in the coup. When asked about these theories, D’Angelo pointed to the public summary of an internal investigation which said that the board acted “within its broad discretion” to fire Altman. He declined further comment on any OpenAI-related questions.
Quora has dealt with other AI controversies, especially when it comes to machine-generated answers. Some users have complained that the quality of content of the site has degraded, becoming a mush of AI slop. In one viral example, an AI-generated Quora answer stated that eggs could be melted. Google, which sources content from Quora in its answer boxes, then amplified the response.
D’Angelo downplayed the criticism. “There's always room to do better on showing better answers,” he said. “Sometimes it's not going to work well and people will be unhappy. But on average, we're quite confident that the AI answers have been a net positive to Quora.”
While Poe has a distinct identity from Quora, D’Angelo said that he never really considered starting a new company to follow his AI ambitions. “It was my full time job and I couldn't just leave and start another company,” he said.
Instead, D’Angelo said he wanted to leverage the talent and structure he had already assembled at Quora, especially as the AI environment moves at a blistering speed. Plus, some of the original source code he wrote for Quora is built into Poe’s foundation. “If it was a new startup, starting from scratch, you might spend the whole first year building up a team that good,” he said. “This was a technology wave and opportunity where we needed to move very, very fast.”
Now the plan is expansion. Building Poe was like “graduating” to becoming a two-product company, D’Angelo told Forbes, akin to Google’s first steps beyond web search. To get it done, the company needed to overcome the “organizational inertia” it had built up over several years. But now that he’s learned how to navigate that change, he doesn’t want to stop there.
“It took a lot of willpower,” he said. “My expectation long term is we should not be only a two-product company. We should continue to build new products.”

title: OpenAI Says Its Pulling ChatGPT Voice ‘Sky’ That Sounds Like Scarlett Johansson
text:
Topline
ChatGPT maker OpenAI on Monday said it is working to drop a voice that sounds like actress Scarlett Johansson, days after the company debuted its new AI voice assistant as part of a major upgrade to its flagship chatbot that intensifies competition with the likes of Apple’s Siri and Amazon’s Alexa.
Key Facts
OpenAI said it is “working to pause the use” of one of the voices used in an audible version of ChatGPT in a post on X, formerly Twitter, early Monday morning.
“We’ve heard questions about how we chose the voices in ChatGPT, especially Sky,” OpenAI said, adding that the voice will be paused until it can address the questions.
Sky is one of the five voices OpenAI debuted as part of its latest AI model, GPT-4o, which powers the company’s hallmark product ChatGPT and allows users to use their voice to interact with the bot and receive responses in kind.
Sky drew widespread attention for its striking similarity to Johansson, particularly her role as an AI voice assistant in the movie Her.
OpenAI itself has acknowledged the vocal similarities between Sky and Johansson but stressed the voice “is not an imitation of Scarlett Johansson” and belongs to “a different professional actress using her own natural speaking voice.”
OpenAI CTO Mira Murati told The Verge Sky is not designed to sound like Johansson either and that the company has had the voices prepared for some time.

Crucial Quote
OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman cryptically posted the word “her” on X after the update and voices were revealed. The tweet was widely received as a reference to the film in which Johansson lends her voice to the role of a virtual assistant. Altman has previously said Her is one of his favorite movies.
What We Don’t Know
While OpenAI is keen to rule out Johansson as the source for Sky, the company said it is unwilling to reveal who is the vocal talent driving the product. “To protect their privacy, we cannot share the names of our voice talents,” OpenAI wrote in a blog. The company stressed it believes “AI voices should not deliberately mimic a celebrity’s distinctive voice.”
News Peg
The GPT-4o upgrade is the latest iteration of OpenAI’s powerful GPT4 model, the driving force powering its ChatGPT chatbot. The company says the upgrade is faster and boosts functionality across text, audio and vision and will be free to all users. The introduction of a voice assistant feature firmly entrenches the company as solid competition for tech giants, expanding the threat it already poses in spaces like generative AI and search engines. In particular, the voice assistant feature for ChatGPT places OpenAI in more direct competition with the other digital voice assistants including Google Assistant, Apple’s Siri and Amazon’s Alexa.
What To Watch For
To get the five voices, OpenAI said it “worked with industry-leading casting and directing professionals to narrow down over 400 submissions before selecting the 5 voices,” with actors flying into San Francisco last June and July for their recording sessions. Each received “above top-of-market rates” for their work, OpenAI said, adding that “even more” voice options will be launched in the future.
Tangent
Johansson has already been the subject of AI mimicry online. In November, she sued an AI app developer for using her name and likeness in an online ad and reportedly she was recently named alongside Conan O’Brien and singer Ariana Grande as an example in a proposed class action against an AI startup accused of misappropriating celebrities' voices.
Forbes Valuation
Altman has an estimated net worth of $1 billion. Altman’s fortune does not come from OpenAI, however, as has no equity in the company, and instead he owes his fortune and billionaire status to a series of valuable investments. This includes stakes in recently floated Reddit, fintech Stripe and nuclear fusion effort Helion. Altman founded social mapping company Loopt and served as partner and president at startup accelerator Y Combinator before starting OpenAI.

Wall Street bets on stellar quarterly results from Nvidia
"There is a lot riding on Nvidia's earnings. It is the most important stock in the sector," said Will Rhind, founder and CEO of GraniteShares, which runs an ETF that invests in the chip firm.
By Arsheeya Bajwa
Wall Street is betting on a blowout quarterly report from Nvidia on Wednesday, with its stock near record highs as investors look for evidence that the AI chipmaker can maintain its explosive growth and stay ahead of rivals.
The results will be the latest test for Wall Street's picks-and-shovels trade that has turned Nvidia into the biggest winner of the generative AI boom, thanks to its chips that are essential in powering technology such as Google's Gemini to OpenAI's ChatGPT.
"There is a lot riding on Nvidia's earnings. It is the most important stock in the sector," said Will Rhind, founder and CEO of GraniteShares, which runs an ETF that invests in the chip firm.
A more than six-fold surge in its shares since the start of 2023 has made Nvidia Wall Street's third-most valuable firm, worth more than $2.30 trillion.
Its 89% stock surge so far in 2024 has helped lift the broader market, and Nvidia now accounts for 5% of the S&P 500, according to LSEG data.
Analyst expectations for Nvidia's future earnings have climbed even faster than its shares. That last left the stock trading at about 35 times expected earnings, down from a peak of over 80 last June, according to LSEG data.
Nvidia's staggering valuation might yet have room to grow. "It is undervalued relative to where forecasts are going," Rhind said.
Analysts on average see Nvidia reporting a 242% jump in revenue to $24.60 billion for the fiscal quarter ending in April, according to LSEG data as of May 17. Its sales in the second quarter are expected to rise almost 97%, the data showed.
Analysts see it reporting net income of $12.83 billion in the first quarter, up from $2.04 billion a year ago.
For several quarters, demand for Nvidia's AI processors has outpaced the number of chips that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, its contract manufacturer, has been able to make.
"The only thing really holding Nvidia back right now is supply," said Inge Heydorn, a partner at investment firm G.P. Bullhound, which owns Nvidia shares.
Investors are also concerned about restrictions by Washington on exports of Nvidia's top-shelf AI chips to China.
Investors are awaiting updates on chips Nvidia is developing for the Chinese market after export curbs reduced its revenue share from China to about 9% of sales in the fourth quarter, from about 22% share in the third.
After several quarters of three-fold growth in its revenue last year, Nvidia is also grappling with tough comparisons.
"As the numbers get bigger, you're up against the law of big numbers, and that percentage beat starts to become less and less," BNP Paribas Exane analyst David O'Connor said.
Rising prices of high-bandwidth memory chips used in its AI semiconductors could also dent margins at Nvidia, with analysts expecting adjusted gross margin of 75.8% in the second quarter, compared with expectations of about 77% in the first.
Gross margins might take a slight hit from "memory costs going up and increasing," said G.P. Bullhound's Heydorn.
Overall, analysts remain confident about Nvidia's growth as technology heavyweights from Microsoft to Meta Platforms boost spending on data centers by billions of dollars in the race for generative AI.
Global spending on cloud infrastructure services is likelyto increase by 20% in 2024 compared with 18% in 2023, according to research firm Canalys.
"Capital expenditures from Big Tech remains high. Despite their efforts to explore alternative or in-house chips, their options are restricted by both limited supply capacity and the challenge of surpassing Nvidia's proven performance," said Ido Caspi, an analyst at Global X ETFs.
"We still view Nvidia as the industry leader for the foreseeable future."

title: Microsoft to unveil AI devices and features ahead of developer conference - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet

Microsoft to unveil AI devices and features ahead of developer conference
After Intel's processors dominated the personal computer market for decades, Qualcomm and other makers of lower-power Arm components have tried to compete in the Windows-PC market.
By Max A. Cherney
SEATTLE: Microsoft plans to announce several pieces of hardware and software related to consumer devices on Monday at an event at its Redmond, Washington, campus.
The Windows maker is expected to reveal a new version of its Surface Pro tablet and Surface Laptop that feature Qualcomm chips based on Arm Holdings' architecture.
After Intel's processors dominated the personal computer market for decades, Qualcomm and other makers of lower-power Arm components have tried to compete in the Windows-PC market.
The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chips include a so-called neural processing unit that is designed to accelerate AI-focused applications, such as Microsoft's Copilot software.
Microsoft's product event, a day before the start of its annual developer conference, is open to journalists and industry analysts who attend in person. It will not be live-streamed.
Microsoft aims to extend its early advantage in the race to produce AI tools that consumers are willing to pay for. Its partnership with ChatGPT maker OpenAI allowed it to jump ahead of Alphabet, as other Big Tech companies race to dominate the emerging field.
Last week, OpenAI and Alphabet's Google showcased dueling AI technologies that can respond via voice in real time and be interrupted, both hallmarks of realistic voice conversations that AI voice assistants have found challenging. Google also announced it was rolling out several generative AI features to its lucrative search engine.
The PC industry has been under increasing pressure from Apple since the company launched its custom chips based on designs from Arm and ditched Intel's processors. The Apple-designed processors have given Mac computers superior battery life and speedier performance than rivals' chips that use more energy.
Microsoft tapped Qualcomm to lead the effort to move the Windows operating system to Arm's chip designs in 2016. Qualcomm has exclusivity on Microsoft Windows devices that expires this year. Other chip designers such as Nvidia have efforts under way to make their own Arm-based PC chips, Reuters has previously reported.
(Reporting by Max A. Cherney in Seattle; Additional reporting by Noel Randewich in Oakland, California; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

title: Council Post: Navigating The AI Revolution In Marketing
text:
Andrew Boni is CEO of Iterable.
In modern marketing, AI is more than just a buzzword—it’s a key driver of success. According to one recent report, 98% of marketers use AI tools such as ChatGPT in some capacity in their jobs, and 64% of marketers consider them very important to success in the next 12 months.
These numbers show the impact AI is already having on our jobs and how much more it will have going forward. Yet this fundamental shift isn’t a simple process. Marketers will have to navigate the complexities of AI adoption carefully to unlock the transformative potential of this new technology.
Personalization Potential
One of the best examples of AI’s utility in marketing is how it can tailor unique messaging content, images, timing and channels based on individual preferences. The result is a better consumer experience through more relevant and useful messaging.
We’re talking about something that goes beyond mere personalization, like attaching a customer’s name to an email. This is true individualization: the ability to generate unique messages or images for millions of people. GenAI data can help us determine the best time to deliver messages as well as the best channel for each individual. Some people prefer push notifications over texts or emails, for example.
Obviously, there need to be checks in the process to make sure that everything stays on-brand. But if we do it right, it provides value to our customers and helps cut through the daily noise of business. Think of the dozens (or hundreds) of emails, text messages and push notifications we all find waiting every morning. By leveraging AI, we can improve the quality of the messages that consumers want to receive.
Trust Through Transparency
It’s easy to think of AI tools as black boxes, spitting out recommendations through some mysterious process of data analysis and deduction. But it’s important to build transparency into the process to build trust and drive adoption.
As an example, one of the AI-powered features we have launched optimizes the send time of a message to maximize engagement. Having to spend time figuring out the best time to send every message was a big friction point for our users. Now, we have systems that can make good predictions based on past engagement data.
But as someone who uses the platform, you naturally want to know why this particular time was recommended or why a particular type of product is best for the end user. Marketers need to have visibility into why AI makes specific recommendations, and providing the rationale behind AI decisions will help overcome adoption challenges.
You’re Only As Good As Your Data
The performance of AI models is only as good as the data used to train them. To truly harness the power of AI to deliver exceptional customer experiences, you need rich, diverse and reliable customer data. Without high-quality inputs, even the most sophisticated AI systems will struggle to generate meaningful insights and personalized recommendations.
Imagine you're an online retailer looking to leverage AI to enhance your customer journey. If your customer data is incomplete, outdated, or siloed across different platforms, your AI initiatives will likely fall short of expectations and your AI models may struggle to generate accurate product recommendations or personalized marketing messages. Stale or incomplete data can lead to irrelevant or even inappropriate suggestions.
To get the maximum out of AI, you need to invest in data integration and management processes that break down silos and provide a unified view of your customers. By centralizing and standardizing your data, you can create a solid foundation for AI to work its magic, enabling more accurate predictions, personalized recommendations, and optimized customer interactions.
By ensuring the highest possible data quality today, we can maximize the performance and reliability of AI systems moving forward, enabling them to deliver more valuable insights and better support decision-making processes.
A Transformative Technological Revolution
AI is unlocking possibilities in marketing that we couldn't have imagined even a year ago. To put this into perspective, think back to when Apple unveiled the iPhone in January 2007. At the time, few people—perhaps with the exception of Steve Jobs—could have predicted the profound impact smartphones would have on our lives. The iPhone revolutionized how we communicate, work and entertain ourselves, giving rise to entirely new industries like the app store and mobile gaming.
Just as the iPhone opened up a new world, AI has the potential to change how we engage with customers from top to bottom. Who knows exactly where it will take us in the next few years—let alone the next decade—but we can be sure those who embrace this technology will be positioned to thrive.

title: Council Post: HR Has A Chance To Lead The AI Revolution
text:
Michael Brainard is the CEO & Founder of Brainard Strategy, a management consulting firm specializing in executive leadership development.
AI is set to revolutionize HR. This means HR leaders have a chance to get out in front by strategically designing how AI will impact their people, performance and cultures.
A Brief History Of Talent Management Software
In the early 2000s, I was consulting with many L&D and HR teams as they sought to either design or re-design performance management processes, application tracking systems and learning and development systems.
At the time, the surge in this type of work was being driven by either:
• a recent implementation of Performance Management software that was intended to make the lives of managers easier, but was mostly met with resistance from those managers, or
• a plan to launch a Performance Management and/or Learning Management System in their organizations.
I received almost daily calls from HR clients seeking help to either assist with the change management around the above systems, or design the processes just prior to—or "more candidly"—just after implementation. It was my experience that HR generally became a "fast-follower" relative to those systems, while the software companies were driving the disruption. But whether leading or "fast following," there is no doubt that these Talent Management platforms brought about significant changes in how HR functioned and was perceived.
To understand how this situation applies to today, we first have to go back to the 1990s. In Josh Bersin's analysis for Forbes (subscription required): "In the late 1990s as the 'war for talent' increased, companies started to snatch up these new talent management systems, focused on automating the processes of recruiting, performance appraisal, and online learning. The talent management [software] market quickly grew, reaching over $2 billion by 2007, and we saw growth rates of double digits year after year."
Today the Talent Management software market continues to grow, with much of that growth driven by use of video and incremental innovation—until now.
AI's integration into the Talent Management platforms will be yet another test, just like the early 2000s: Will the software companies lead, or will HR leaders?
The AI Revolution And HR
From a Talent Acquisition perspective, AI-powered algorithms can analyze resumes, screen candidates and even conduct initial interviews. AI algorithms can match candidates with job openings based on skills, experience and cultural fit, leading to better hires and reduced turnover.
From a Performance Management and L&D perspective, AI tools can track employee performance metrics in real time, providing insights into productivity, engagement and potential areas for improvement. This can lead to more objective performance evaluations and targeted development plans. AI-driven personalized learning platforms can then recommend training courses and development opportunities tailored to each employee's skills, goals and learning style.
A case study: Just before COVID, my company was asked to perform a needs assessment for a large organization with very diverse job types. Traditionally, this would require hours of focus groups, interviews and surveys, as well as data analyses. Our findings would then suggest targeted content for different types of employees and leaders. The needs assessment alone was set to take three months to complete. We partnered with our client to think differently.
Their current Talent Management systems actually had ample (under-leveraged) data that we leveraged, along with predictive statistics, to create targeted learning needs maps based on time in position, prior training, level and job requirements, etc. This work took us about four weeks to complete. I recently spoke with the same client and she mentioned that this work we did, using predictive techniques and existing data over a matter of weeks, could now be done in minutes by leveraging AI in their existng LMS.
Like a large language model, statistics have been "packaged" in such a way that the data analysts can now type in a desired outcome, and the LMS does the rest, producing targeted learning needs to the L&D leader.
HR's Moment Of Opportunity
AI can significantly advance the strategic value HR brings to organizations. But without strategic deployment and thoughtful HR leadership, I wonder if AI deployment into our existing Talent Management systems will help or exacerbate existing challenges.
By using AI to advance the use of predictive analytics, HR can get out in front of the strategic workforce questions organizations are facing. HR must not be a "fast follower" this time, but must seize this moment in time to strategically lead their organizations. This is the time to earn the proverbial "seat at the table."
Let’s focus on just one of the many opportunities AI offers HR leaders: HR could lead American companies to eliminate the pay gap for women in the workforce.
Using AI tools, we can analyze pay and demographic data to identify discrepancies. We can then analyze promotion rates, performance evaluations and salary negotiation outcomes across gender lines. Then, using AI, we can model scenarios and impacts of correcting those discrepencies across an organization. We could even use AI to monitor ongoing hiring, promotion, pay and performance data so as to never enable pay gaps in the future.
I strongly believe that AI could be leveraged to eliminate this problem tomorrow—with strong HR leadership.
Final Thoughts
Overall, AI has massive potential in HR. However, if HR is not strategically at the helm of deploying AI into existing technology platforms for overall organizational health, engagement and productivity, then the HR community will have again missed an opportunity in history, just like the early 2000s.
