title: Council Post: CIO’s 2024 Checklist: Generative AI, Digital Transformation And More
text:
Linh Lam, CIO at Jamf.
In 2023, the cybersecurity industry experienced massive shifts when it comes to the technology we use and how we use it. Many CIOs and security teams were left in a state of information overload, trying to effectively leverage automation in enterprise operations while simultaneously attempting to navigate a whirlwind of regulatory and policy news and keep employees happy to avoid skilling and/or workforce shortages.
Needless to say, CIOs have a lot on their plate in 2024.
Developing a list of priorities can seem like a daunting task for CIOs, and understandably so—with new innovations hitting the market daily that seem to all be the “next big thing,” 3,000 vendors to choose from once you decide what’s worth the investment, the rise of regulations and the tightening of budgets, knowing what’s important can start to seem impossible.
As technology continues to evolve, so will the relationship between IT and security teams. The CIO must ensure all digital technology leaders are on the same page with a clear vision. So, now comes the question to end all questions: where do you start?
Embracing Digital Transformation
In 2024, CIOs should prioritize enabling digital transformation and strengthening cybersecurity.
In driving digital transformation, CIOs can provide a seamless experience for customers, partners and employees. Embracing emerging technologies—such as automation, AI and analytics to optimize operations—unlock insights and personalize engagements across every touchpoint while ensuring clear communication across internal teams should take top billing to ensure a quality experience for everyone.
That last piece on clear communication should not be overlooked. In addition to using emerging technologies to benefit customers, CIOs should ensure their employees have the opportunity to understand and benefit from innovations as well. Training employees on how to leverage new technologies safely and responsibly is crucial for fostering an environment of true innovation.
In addition to embracing digital transformation, CIOs must remain wary about optimizing what they have in their architecture. Simply adding emerging technologies for the sake of adding emerging technologies is an inefficient way of embracing digital transformation.
CIOs are always under pressure to rationalize their software usage and total spend to their organizations. Having the ability to speak intelligently about such emerging technologies, what software the emerging technologies have the potential to replace, clearly laying out the benefits and being honest about the drawbacks will remain critical to success for CIOs throughout the rest of the year and beyond.
Adhering To Compliance Requirements
While embracing emerging technologies, it is also critical to double down on cybersecurity and compliance to maintain the trust of stakeholders.
While much has been made about the SEC breach reporting requirements, we must acknowledge that this very well could just be the tip of the iceberg when it comes to regulatory compliance. Abiding by these regulations is inevitably going to come to the forefront in 2024 and future years.
By delivering on those two critical pillars of digital transformation and strong cybersecurity, CIOs can achieve their vision of empowering people with technology that puts them in charge of their experiences and lives. With the right strategies and investments in 2024, we can continue to build on the strong foundation we have established in enabling secure and seamless work from anywhere.
Navigating The World Of Automation
Stop me if you’ve heard this before: Generative AI should remain a high priority when it comes to empowering customers and employees. People have grown to expect a seamless and intuitive experience when doing business or getting work done. Leveraging generative AI capabilities to enable self-service, personalize engagements and simplify complex processes will allow stakeholders the ability to work smarter, not harder.
While generative AI is exciting, we also must acknowledge that cybersecurity should remain mission-critical. Customers and partners trust us to secure their data and operations, and it is on us to ensure we are maturing our cyber defenses through leading technology, automation and best practices.
CIOs’ focus should be on ensuring we are developing win-win AI applications that augment human capabilities and foster trust. With the right strategy and investments in responsible AI, we can provide customers and employees with the automated assistance they need, while continuing to safeguard transparency, security and human oversight.
Same Thing, Different Year?
While the remainder of 2024 will undoubtedly have changes in store for both the cybersecurity industry and the CIO community in particular, one thing remains certain: digital transformation, the automation experience and robust security will remain ongoing priorities as we evolve in step with emerging technologies.
Even as technologies progress rapidly, the CIO’s commitment should remain constant: to pursue digital transformation and heightened cybersecurity through creative and ethical applications of new capabilities. By adapting intelligently and staying ahead of the curve, we will fulfill our goal of securely enabling exceptional experiences and incredible outcomes.

title: Council Post: No-Code/Low-Code And Generative AI Go Hand In Hand
text:
Praerit Garg is President of Product & Innovation at Smartsheet, the enterprise platform for modern work management.
We’re in the middle of a transformative moment in the workplace with the wide proliferation of generative AI tools. While AI itself is not a new technology (it’s been many years in the making), the rise of generative AI has made what’s old feel new again. Many of us are experiencing AI in our day-to-day lives in a new way, as generative AI technology has been rapidly integrated into the programs and platforms we use at work and home.
Much has already been written about the potential of generative AI to dramatically impact how work gets done. Leaders, too, are well aware of how transformative generative AI could be. According to joint research by MIT Sloan Management Review and the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), almost 85% of leaders surveyed believe AI will enable their companies to get or maintain a competitive advantage.
This is where gaps become clear between the acknowledged potential of generative AI, employees’ perception of it and the way it’s being implemented across organizations. In that same MIT and BCG study, only about 1 in 5 companies had incorporated AI in some offerings or processes. Gallup found that more than half of employees surveyed reported feeling unprepared to work with AI.
Business leaders and employees are fully aware of the presence and power of this technology as well as its ability to unlock potential and productivity. How do we empower companies and users to feel confident and prepared? Adopting no-code/low-code principles while innovating with generative AI technology can help solve this problem.
No-code/low-code technology is also not a new concept and has been somewhat of the “holy grail” of programming for over 40 years. From Excel spreadsheets to HTML, developers have been aiming to lower the skills bar for more people to be able to participate and contribute to technology.
This is exactly the purpose and appeal of no-code/low-code technology—to serve users without requiring them to be developers or technical experts, just as we shouldn’t ask users to assume the role of an AI expert to take full advantage of the potential of the technology.
In that way, generative AI is a technological gift for no-code/low-code platforms. The technology enables users to ask questions or describe their needs conversationally using natural language. They don’t need to learn a new set of terms or a specific technological language for the system to generate the output the user wants.
It can be difficult to know where to start. For tech and product leaders in the no-code/low-code industry evaluating how better to integrate generative AI into your solution, my top piece of advice is to focus on solving customer pain points within established workflows.
What do I mean by this? By building generative AI capabilities that fit into a user’s already established workflow (and not asking them to learn something new or adopt a new process), we can empower even more people to unlock potential with this transformative technology.
For example, my company, Smartsheet, offers a no-code solution—in our case, it’s a work management platform. You don’t need any specialized skills to be able to configure a system for managing your projects, programs and processes. However, there are still common pain points that we hear from customers that generative AI can help solve without needing to adapt to an entirely new workflow.
We’ve gotten customer feedback that writing formulas within the product can be difficult and tedious. That’s why an early focus of our generative AI innovation was to help users build formulas by simply describing in natural human language what problem they’re trying to solve, and then the generative AI capability creates the appropriate formula. This means our users are interacting with the AI without feeling intimidated by the assumption they need to learn an entirely new skill—just like the principles of no-code/low-code have shown us.
There is still so much to learn about the potential of generative AI technology and all of the different ways it will transform the way we work. By approaching this technology with the no-code/low-code mindset and incorporating it into our tools and platforms in a way that applies to users’ accustomed workflows, the barrier to using and understanding it will be lowered.
By making generative AI easier to use and innovate with, we can close the understanding gap and empower employees to unlock potential faster.

title: Council Post: Selection Is Strategy: A Critical Role For The CIO In Your AI Journey
text:
Narinder Singh is the CEO of LookDeep Health and previously a founder of Appirio, a pioneer in cloud computing.
With the dawn of the age of AI-centric enterprise software, technology selection feels more antiquated than ever. Yet the cost of a poor choice today can have exponentially greater consequences than in any previous era.
The RFP (Request for Proposal) originated near the dawn of industrialization; technology made more manageable its hundreds of questions and responses from dozens of vendors. Not surprisingly, this quickly was applied to the selection of technology itself, and today, it is one of the primary ways larger bureaucratic organizations select software.
The critiques of this approach are many. By now it feels as normal and hopeless as criticizing the tax code or healthcare system. AI raises the stakes of this because of its exponential potential. Just as the dawn of the internet could doom the business models of entire companies, AI can additionally completely disrupt entire functional areas of every company—and can do it faster than we’ve ever seen.
In the past, the cost of picking the wrong solution was impactful but limited. Perhaps you would deploy a few months slower or execute marginally less efficiently. Despite the most dramatic of claims, no one believes picking the wrong ERP could reduce your operating income by 10%, or that picking the right CRM will increase your sales by 30%. The intensity of the selection process felt it was exactly “because the stakes are so low.”
Yet AI redefines the boundaries of what software can do. What today takes 1000 people could take 500—or 50—depending on the quality of the AI and how it is integrated into the process enabled by software. In this world, CIOs must not allow their organization to continue the practices of the past. Far more than with the emergence of the internet, they control and guide the ability of their organizations to use technology in a way that can directly affect the top and bottom lines.
Here are five steps CIOs in every industry should institute to adapt.
1. Stack the deck against long-term contracts (reserve option value). AI is evolving so quickly it’s nearly impossible to see who will be the innovator in redefining the boundaries of software. The option value of being able to switch horses has never been higher, and longer contracts have never been more expensive.
2. Integration over just all-in-one. For a generation, debates between the virtues of software suites versus best-of-breed ran rampant. Both categories (mostly) resolved the problem with strong integration. This will become essential with AI algorithms. Vendors proposing they can do everything are dangerous vehicles of lockin. It’s unlikely the same company will build the best AI algorithm for customer support and supply chain optimization or for assisting surgeries in the operating room and identifying the highest-risk babies in the NICU. Platform shifts require openness to navigate uncertainty.
3. Adopt PLG (Product Led Growth) concepts. Open-source tools allow developers to learn the capabilities of a technology before placing a large financial bet on it. RFPs are cast aside or become formalities because the buyer has already used and understands the product deeply. This approach has not been relevant to large enterprise software, but even here, we can adapt. Use focused demo scenarios where your team is allowed to place hands on keyboards without restriction for days or even weeks. Provide flexibility to allow your prospective vendors to differentiate their capabilities, but insist you will be part of the process. The speed at which they can move and the experience your teams have with the product are far more meaningful than hundreds of questions about the capabilities.
4. Dive deep into AI to understand capability and trajectory. For the next several years, last year’s AI capabilities will feel trivial. You must understand both AI capabilities and their trajectory. Show me how/where AI is in your product today (not a concept video). Explain what data you use to train, validate and improve your algorithms on an ongoing basis. Tell me where they work less well and if/how you will address this. It may be difficult to validate the content of their algorithms, but the process of innovation can be revealed. The more open your vendor is to you and the industry (publications, peer-reviewed conferences, etc.), the less chance you are being sold the next Theranos.
5. Ban the traditional RFP. Ask ten open-ended questions, use AI to parse the results and use it as the beginning of your hands-on product-centric process (see #3). Your historical 137 requirement RFPs are the equivalent of lawyers sending thousands of documents to hide the one they don’t want you to see. You have added noise to the process and made it harder to identify the real signal. Your initial step is to understand the strategy and position of the products you are evaluating and how they contrast with one another. From there, the hands-on phase will allow you to build trust and detailed understanding you can use with and across vendors. Forty-two questions upfront on security seldom serve your best interests in understanding their security readiness. There are multiple ways to construct a new process, and nearly all of them will serve you better than starting with a traditional RFP. Year-long evaluation processes reveal poor execution in your IT organizations.
Ultimately, there will be AI tools to help with product selection. They will discover a vendor's stated capabilities and position in the market and allow your selection process to focus on private information. Interactions that reveal more about their pace of innovation, trust and credibility and approach to partnership. Transitioning from the traditional RFP process will help you better understand vendors' capabilities and improve your ability to execute with any AI technology to create an advantage for your business.
CEOs will demand CIOs who seize this moment to transform their approach to working with AI vendors—your top and bottom lines could depend on it.

title: Council Post: Why Limiting AI Literacy Training To Your IT Team Is A Big Mistake
text:
Joseph Ours leads the AI Strategy and Modern Software Delivery Practices at Centric Consulting.
Over an eight-year period, Rite Aid used facial recognition in hundreds of its pharmacy chain locations. The idea was simple. It would use facial recognition to “keep persons of interest out of (Rite Aid’s) stores,” the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said, in what it has dubbed a “covert surveillance” program.
To do this, Rite Aid authorized the creation of a database of images that identified people who had allegedly engaged in or attempted criminal activity at one of its stores. It logged a person’s name, birth year and suspected activity. When a match occurred, the store’s staff was responsible for asking the person to leave and calling the police, if necessary.
Not only had consumers not been told they were being surveilled, but the facial recognition flawed, leading to false identifications and humiliated customers and causing an investigation and FTC ban on using the technology for five years.
At the most basic level, AI literacy training could have prevented most, if not all, of Rite Aid’s debacle. AI literacy is something that not every business actively thinks about, but they should.
Why Does AI Literacy Matter?
AI literacy is more than understanding terminology. At its core, it involves having the skills and competencies needed to use AI technologies and applications successfully. That means recognizing AI, understanding its underlying principles and impacts and knowing how to use it effectively and legally.
Before the proliferation of generative AI tools to the average consumer, it may have been fine for just your company’s tech team to understand these concepts. Today, AI features are embedded into everyday tools, applications and processes. While technical teams can bring innovation, businesspeople bring what the market wants and needs. Marrying the two requires that everyone understands AI.
Leaders need to know AI’s capabilities and risks so they can appropriately deploy AI and maximize its return for the organization. Everyone else in the organization needs to know how to use it to ensure they get the most out of it. But, as in the Rite Aid scenario, they also need to know how to avoid misusing AI.
Failing to train the organization is like putting your great-grandfather in front of Google and telling him to go ahead and use it. He wouldn’t know where to start and would be naive about the harm it can cause. AI is no different.
In fact, in the FTC complaint against Rite Aid, one of the failures outlined by the pharmacy chain was to “adequately train employees tasked with operating facial recognition technology in its stores and flag that the technology could generate false positives,” as its press release noted.
Risks Are Inherent, But AI Literacy Can Minimize Them
In any emerging technology, risk is inherent. That is, it cannot be separated or eliminated. But when AI isn’t proactively understood and addressed before deployment, you open your company to significant harm.
Take, for example, one prominent company that experienced unintended impacts as a direct result of lack of AI literacy.
Wanting to offer customers a cool and futuristic car buying experience, a Chevy dealership added an AI-powered chatbot to its website. Consumers were able to trick the chatbot into acting against the dealership’s interests, ultimately agreeing to sell a car for $1.
While this was a non-legally binding agreement (despite the language “and that’s a legally binding offer—no takesies backsies”), the post went viral, the dealership was embarrassed, and it could have faced financial losses all due to an inadequate understanding of AI and the allure of using it to enhance the customer experience.
You can’t responsibly adopt AI without first instilling AI literacy throughout your organization.
What Do Companies Want With AI?
Our clients want the benefits of AI, from increased productivity to enhanced user experience and faster times to market. What they don’t want is to be in the news for poorly implemented AI.
To deliver this, AI literacy is a vital skill set, and like with honing any skill set, training is key.
The Basics Of AI Literacy Training
We’ve found that major insurers, educational institutions and even courts need to know the basics, that is, capabilities, limitations, ethical considerations and responsible use. AI literacy isn’t something you have to tackle on your own.
Recognizing the importance of AI literacy, a Fortune 10 company who pioneered e-commerce and logistics engaged us for AI literacy training to ensure their business partners understood how an AI initiative would benefit them, as well as to ensure appropriate use to maximize the value AI could bring.
At a minimum, AI literacy training should include:
• An Introduction To AI Models: Gain an understanding of AI in its historical context and look at various AI models. This foundational knowledge will set the stage for a deeper dive.
• Generative AI: This is a big one because generative AI is so pervasive and what people generally think of when they think of AI. Help people understand how AI systems can be used effectively to help stay ahead of the curve.
• Broad Capabilities: Go beyond the scope of generative AI to help people understand other AI capabilities, from machine learning and natural language processing to computer vision, and more.
• Responsible AI Practices: Take time to learn about ethical implications of AI, from bias to fairness, transparency and accountability. This will help emphasize the need to ensure AI benefits the company without causing undue harm.
• The AI Project Life Cycle: What are the practical aspects of AI project implementation? Everyone in a company should have at least a foundational knowledge of the life cycle from problem formulation to data collection, model training, deployment and monitoring.
AI literacy training can give leadership and employees the foundation they need to complete day-to-day tasks, make decisions and get the most out of AI. The more leadership and employees understand about AI, the less likely they are to become a cautionary tale that lives in infamy.

title: Council Post: Unleashing The Power Of Retrieval-Augmented Generation For Medium-Sized Businesses
text:
Scott Wassmer, Global President – Appnovation.
Many medium-sized business leaders are constantly on the lookout for technologies that can catapult them into the future, ensuring they remain competitive, innovative and efficient. One such advancement is the integration of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) into their operational and strategic frameworks.
My company develops generative AI products for many of our clients. Recently we've been adding the additional layer of RAG to the products we develop and have seen enhancement beyond the standard implementation of generative AI platforms.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
At its core, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a sophisticated technique in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) that combines the strengths of two approaches: information retrieval and generative modeling. Here's a look at these components and how RAG works:
• Information retrieval: This component involves searching a dataset or knowledge base to find pieces of information that are relevant to a given query or context. The retrieved information serves as a foundation or context for generating an accurate and informed response, as opposed to standard generative AI models that can only deliver information based on the data they were trained on.
• Generative modeling: After retrieving the relevant information, a generative AI model uses it to generate text, answers or content. This model leverages the retrieved data to produce outputs that are not only relevant and coherent but also enriched with the detailed context provided by the retrieved documents.
By combining RAG and GenAI, you get the ability to create context that evolves based on new data and inputs (RAG) with the ability to deliver information in a format that makes the most sense to the end user (GenAI).
How RAG Works
1. Input processing: The process begins when a query or prompt is inputted into the system. This query serves as the basis for both the retrieval and generation phases.
2. Document retrieval: The retrieval component searches through a predefined dataset, such as Wikipedia or a specialized knowledge base, to find content that is relevant to the input query. The criteria for relevance can be based on semantic similarity, keyword matching or other sophisticated matching algorithms.
3. Content generation: The generative model then uses the retrieved documents along with the original query to generate a response. This model synthesizes information from both sources to create a comprehensive answer that reflects the input's intent and the contextual insights from the retrieved data.
4. Output delivery: The final generated content is delivered as the system's response to the query. This response aims to be more accurate, informative and contextually rich than what could be produced by a stand-alone generative model.
The Strategic Advantage For Medium-Sized Businesses
Medium-sized businesses are uniquely positioned to leverage RAG for several reasons. They possess the agility to implement innovative technologies quickly, the size to scale solutions efficiently and the need to compete with larger entities in knowledge-driven areas. Here are the key benefits RAG can offer:
1. Enhanced decision-making: RAG empowers decision-makers with access to a broader range of information and data-driven insights. By tapping into extensive external databases, RAG provides a comprehensive understanding of market trends, customer behaviors and competitive landscapes.
2. Improved customer experience: RAG enables the creation of AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants that provide personalized and context-aware responses.
3. Streamlining operations: From optimizing supply chain logistics based on real-time market data to automating routine tasks with precision, RAG can streamline various operational processes. This can result in cost savings, improved productivity and the ability to reallocate resources to strategic initiatives.
4. Innovation in product development: RAG can inform product development, helping businesses to stay ahead of the curve and meet market demands with innovative solutions that resonate with their target audience.
5. Competitive intelligence: Keeping a pulse on the competition is vital, and RAG offers an edge by analyzing large volumes of data to uncover competitive strategies, market positions and potential threats. This intelligence is instrumental in formulating robust competitive strategies and identifying unique value propositions.
Implementing RAG: Considerations And Steps Forward
While the benefits of RAG are vast, successful implementation requires careful planning and execution. Businesses must evaluate their existing data infrastructure, ensure they have the right talent in place and choose RAG solutions that align with their specific needs and goals. It's also crucial to consider the ethical and privacy implications of using large-scale data, ensuring compliance with all relevant regulations.
Partnering with knowledgeable organizations can smooth this transition. Consider a partner with expertise in technology selection, integration and scaling, alongside strategic advice to maximize the impact of RAG on your business. When looking for a partner, always ask to see how that partner has implemented RAG in the past and try to understand their overall experience with GenAI. Beware of companies using AI terms to insinuate expertise rather than having it—this requires extra due diligence when finding the right partner.
Getting started with RAG can lead to several challenges due to the complexity of the technology and the need for significant data resources. In addition to this, cultural resistance because of job and workflow disruption can be a major challenge within any organization as we're seeing with other generative AI projects.
In order to solve some of these challenges, I'd recommend that any company looking to incorporate RAG into their content ecosystem focus on the following steps:
1. Start with a pilot project to show the viability within your company.
2. Focus on data management to ensure the information you retreive is based on a solid data foundation.
3. Implement an effective change management process so that everyone is involved and understand the goals and outcomes you're looking to achieve.
I think retrieval-augmented generation represents a significant leap forward in the application of AI for business, particularly for medium-sized businesses. By harnessing the power of RAG, businesses can not only enhance their current operations but also pave the way for future growth and success in the digital age.

title: Council Post: Betting On AI: How Artificial Intelligence Levels The Playing Field For Everyday Investors
text:
Si Katara, Founder and CEO of TappAlpha.
In the intricate world of personal finance, the game often seems rigged against the everyday investor. With our days already divided among jobs, families and the never-ending treadmill of daily to-dos, who really has the hours needed to decode the stock market? The rules of the game—complex, time-consuming and often opaque—favor those with the resources to either stay glued to Bloomberg terminals or pay someone else to do it.
But what if technology could change the rules? What if artificial intelligence (AI) could shrink the biggest barriers when it comes to accessing the potential of public markets: time, know-how and trust? Here’s how AI isn’t just fitting into the world of finance—it’s poised to revolutionize it for the everyday investors of the world.
The Challenge At Hand
1. The Time Crunch
In the financial leagues, time is the currency most scarce. For those without the luxury to deliberate over spreadsheets or agonize over asset allocations, investment often gets pushed to the back burner, simmering on a low heat of forgotten 401(k)s and neglected brokerage accounts. But neglect in investing is akin to pausing mid-sprint in a marathon—not only do you lose ground, but you also miss the chance to surge ahead when the path clears.
2. The Expertise Gap
Derivatives, covered calls and short sells—these aren't just terms but barriers. They create a club whose membership costs more than just fees—it costs years of learning and loss. Most individual investors lack the Ph.D. in finance that seems almost a prerequisite for modern investment strategies. This knowledge gap can lead to paralyzing inaction or, worse, misguided decisions.
3. The Trust Deficit
In the world of finance, clarity is often obscured by complex fee structures and opaque investment processes. This lack of transparency creates a trust deficit, as everyday investors struggle to fully understand where their money goes and how it's managed. Many are unaware of the total fees extracted from their brokerage accounts—a critical detail that could mean the difference between retiring early or working into their golden years. Establishing clear and transparent financial practices is essential for building trust and empowering investors to make informed decisions that optimize their financial futures.
AI In The Financial Arena
Overcoming The Time Crunch
Consider the immense effort and time required to effectively analyze and execute sophisticated investment strategies—time that most everyday investors simply don't have. AI-driven tools offer a practical solution to this problem. Operating continuously in the background, these systems can analyze huge amounts of data, track real-time market movements, execute trades and make adjustments much faster than any human could. These are tasks that AI is built to do in its sleep. And more importantly, these are tasks it can do while you sleep. This automation lifts a significant burden off the shoulders of investors, enabling a much wider audience to leverage the benefits of sophisticated investment strategies without the intensive time commitment traditionally required.
Bridging The Expertise Gap
AI has the potential to democratize financial wisdom. Through intuitive platforms that provide real-time explanations and context-specific advice, AI can serve as both coach and player in the investment game. It can suggest when to buy into certain stocks or employ strategies like covered calls, all while educating the investor on why these moves do or don’t make sense in simple, jargon-free language.
Restoring Trust
Trust and transparency go hand in hand. AI can help provide not only transparency about such things as fee structures and operating costs but also context around those fee structures for the universe of similar products to see if they're, in fact, competitive. This includes incorporating factors beyond costs, such as value provided in exchange for those costs, in the broader context of how products perform over time and in what kind of market environments. In a nutshell, AI can apply knowledge and context to transparency to give investors confidence to make decisions based on a full and clear understanding, not incomplete or hidden information.
Conclusion
AI’s entrance into finance isn’t just a new player entering an old game—it’s a whole new game. For the everyday investor, AI can serve as the great equalizer, stripping away the complexities of Wall Street and replacing them with straightforward, trustworthy assistance. As AI continues to evolve, it promises not only to adapt to the world of finance but to redefine it, ensuring that everyone—not just the elite—gets a fair shot at financial success.
In this light, AI doesn’t just support investment—it transforms it. By tackling the fundamental issues of time, know-how and trust, AI isn’t just solving problems—it’s setting a new standard for what investing can be. Welcome to the new era of personal finance, where everyone has a chance to be on the winning team.

title: AI Is Changing The Movie Theater Experience… For The Better?
text:
The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming various industries, and the movie theater sector is no exception. From personalized marketing to optimizing operations, AI is enhancing the movie-going experience and helping theaters stay competitive in an increasingly digital world.
Current Uses of AI in Movie Theaters
For customers, movie theaters serve as the face of movies. Consequently, cinemas are the vanguard in movie marketing. Thus, these circuits are leveraging AI for personalized marketing and recommendations: Theaters use AI algorithms to analyze customer data and provide personalized movie recommendations. For example, AMC Theaters employs AI to suggest films based on past viewing habits, leading to increased ticket sales and customer satisfaction. In addition, cinemas are adopting the strategy of many sports teams with dynamic pricing. Theaters have fixed capacity, and an unsold seat is a waste. Thus, they are using AI dynamic pricing to optimize ticket sales and in attempt to maximize available capacity. Regal Cinemas, for instance, uses AI to adjust ticket prices based on demand, time of day, and even seating preferences. This strategy helps maximize revenue and ensures better occupancy rates. Furthermore, cinemas want to enhance customer service. Cinemas deploy AI for customer service. Cinemark Theaters uses chatbots for ticket booking, showtime inquiries, and even to handle customer complaints, providing a seamless and efficient experience for moviegoers. In addition, theaters have discovered a powerful operational use case in predictive maintenance. Theater equipment is specialized and sometimes finicky. By monitoring the performance data of projectors and sound systems, AI can predict when maintenance is needed, reducing downtime and ensuring a high-quality viewing experience for audiences. Finally, who likes lines? Well, surprise, AI is an effective crowd management tool. Given these challenges, theaters are rapidly adopting AI for crowd management and security, particularly for new movie releases. AI surveillance systems analyze foot traffic and crowd patterns to enhance safety and optimize staffing during peak times.
Enhancing the Viewing Experience with AI
Beyond operations, AI is also enhancing the actual movie-viewing experience. Concerned about the audio and visual aspects of a movie? Well, cinemas have you covered through AI in projection and sound systems. Advanced AI algorithms are being used to calibrate projectors and sound systems for optimal performance. IMAX, for instance, uses AI to enhance image and sound quality, tailoring it to specific theater dimensions. Want better movies? Theaters are deploying facial recognition for audience analysis. Through this technology, cinemas (and studios) will gauge audience reactions during a movie. This data can be valuable for feedback to movie studios and for tailoring future movie selections and marketing strategies. Tired of the old 2D experience? Theaters are already shifting to virtual reality (VR) experiences powered by AI. The convergence of these two technologies offers an immersive movie experience that adds a new level of interaction as well as personalization. Theaters are starting to recommend VR content based on customer preferences, providing a personalized and engaging experience that makes each movie viewing experience unique.
AI in Theater Management and Operations
Back-end operations of movie theaters is another critical area for theaters, especially to streamline processes and reducing costs. First and foremost, consider inventory management. AI systems help in managing concessions and merchandise inventory efficiently. Algorithms predict demand trends, helping theaters stock up appropriately and reduce waste. Second, in the age of sustainability, cinemas are confronting the challenge of energy management. Already, circuits use AI for energy management by optimizing heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems based on theater occupancy and external weather conditions. This not only reduces energy costs but also contributes to environmental sustainability. Third, cinemas have unique staff scheduling challenges given the nature of movie times and the labor pool. As a result, more and more theaters are turning to AI for staff scheduling. By leveraging AI tools, theaters have a round-the-clock assistant in staff scheduling that uses real-time data to predict busy periods, ensuring theaters are adequately staffed during peak times and saving labor costs during off-peak hours.
Ethical and Privacy Considerations
While cinemas have a lot of benefits, they also need to consider the potential misuses of AI within theaters. Facial recognition and data analysis raises concerns about privacy and data security. How much data is enough versus what goes overboard for moviegoers is a delicate balance to maintain as well. Thus, it is crucial for theaters to adhere to strict data protection regulations and be transparent with customers about how their data is being used.
Future Applications of AI in Movie Theaters
Gazing into the short-term future, AI will further transform movie theaters in several ways. To start with, audiences will experience customized viewing. These experiences, fueled by AI, will offer customizable viewing experiences based on each person’s individual preferences. For example, theaters could use AI to adjust the movie's audio-visual elements in real-time, based on audience preferences and reactions to create a 4-D experience. Building on this, individualized targeting is the next frontier for theaters in using AI. Already at the forefront, some cinemas are incorporating more targeted experiences, not a micro-segment level but rather for each specific person. Employing solutions like 3XM Technologies, theaters are leveraging data for dynamic pricing, particularly to incentivize low peak times, as well as rewards matching. That is, understanding each of their customers at level of a best friend to identify precision incentives coupled with individual messaging (i.e., the right context and words) to connect with each movie goer for precision messaging. Next, the convergence of augmented reality (AR) Interactions and AI will create interactive movie posters and displays, offering engaging content such as trailers, behind-the-scenes footage, or interactive games related to the movies. That not only adds to the overall movie experience but also opens some very intriguing doors for lead generation to movie goers who may not ordinarily consider a particular movie. Additionally, cinemas are starting to experiment with data-driven film scheduling. AI will analyze local demographics and viewing trends to assist theaters in scheduling films that are more likely to attract larger audiences in specific locales and at specific times, enabling more efficient use of their existing capacity. Finally, enhanced security measures, sadly, are an increasing concern. AI is already enhancing security measures by identifying suspicious behavior or unattended items to ensure a safer environment for moviegoers. Given recent public area incidents, theaters are rapidly exploring deeper use of these capabilities to improve the safety of their audiences.
AI is set to play a pivotal role in the future of movie theaters, offering innovative solutions to enhance both operational efficiency and the customer experience. As cinemas continue to adopt and integrate AI technologies, they will not only improve their competitiveness but also redefine the movie-going experience. However, this journey must be navigated with careful consideration of ethical and privacy concerns to maintain customer trust and ensure the responsible use of technology.

title: Will Artificial Intelligence Diminish Our Humanity?
text:
Last week, OpenAI introduced GPT-4o, the newest version of its AI chatbot.
One of the things they showed was being able to have an actual conversation with a female-voiced chatbot and even interrupt her at will to tighten the prompt question. The demo also showed that this chatbot had a personality and a playful side.
In the GPT-4o demo, OpenAI's Chief Technology Officer, Mira Murati, and colleagues showed how the new version speaks, understands, and expresses emotions. Watching the demo made it easy to think one was talking to a natural person. The female chatbot was lifelike. Ms. Murati then asked it to analyze what it was looking at.
In the video, a person pointed the phone's camera at a screen displaying computer code and had GPT-4o describe the code and what it can do. In another example, one member of the team asked the chatbot to help him with a math problem and GPT-4o gave him the steps to answer the question. Using a pleasing and conversational voice that spoke deliberately and patiently, it was more like interacting with a tutor.
This conversational chatbot reminds me of a 2013 movie called Her, in which Joaquin Phoenix’s character develops a relationship with a female chat agent, voiced by Scarlett Johansson. In the movie, Mr. Phoenix's character develops a relationship with what today we call a chatbot and experiences feelings and a distinct attachment to this robot character.
One day after OpenAI showed GPT-4o, Google announced its newest Gemini AI Chatbot version. In a keynote presentation at Google I/O, their developer conference held in Mountain View, CA., Google's VP and head of Search, Liz Reid announced an AI overview that they describe as, "Whatever's on your mind, whatever you need to get done, just ask and Google will do the Googling for you."
In one demo, a Google executive used her phone to video a record player arm skipping. Then, she asked Google's Gemini AI, "Why will it not stay in place?" Gemini AI explained that the arm was not balanced and thus would not stay in place.
In another demo, a Google employee scanned a room with her phone and said, "Tell me when you see something that makes a sound" and she then heard, "I see a speaker that hears a sound."
Another one that hit home for me was a demo in which Gemini AI was asked, "Where did I put my glasses?" She got the answer from her phone, which had recorded her movement in the room and told her where to find them.
Google is also integrating its Gemini AI into its other products, including Google Photos. For example, Google Photos can now tell you your license plate number if it has a picture of your plate. It can also help evaluate how your kids are doing with their swimming lessons based on photos and videos of your child in pools, lakes, and ocean waters.
I encourage you to view the videos of OpenAI’s GPT-4o and Google's Gemini, which give more details on what both companies announced and which I believe will have major ramifications for our future.
While I was impressed with the advancements OpenAI and Google have made, especially how Google's Gemini will become their new search engine, I was also somewhat saddened at what I saw in their presentations.
Both companies are developing advanced tools that have the potential to greatly enhance our lives. However, it should be noted that these tools may also have a profound impact on our humanity.
The intersection of human and AI interaction is not merely a frontier of technological innovation but a pivotal juncture redefining our relationships and productivity paradigms. As AI integrates deeper into our personal and professional lives, its influence extends beyond efficiency gains, encroaching upon the essence of human experience. This integration challenges traditional notions of creativity, empathy, and interpersonal connections, areas that were once believed to be exclusively human domains.
The shift in the human-AI paradigm makes us rely more on these AI tools to do almost everything for us. "Doing" is the essence of what makes us human. Rather than relying on robotic AI service agents to handle tasks for us, our humanity is best expressed through learning and directly experiencing the world around us. Our emotions and connections with others are fundamental aspects of this experience.
Yes, this evolution also presents an unparalleled opportunity to augment our capabilities, enabling us to achieve higher productivity levels while fostering a new symbiosis between human intuition and artificial intelligence. The key lies in navigating this delicate balance without diminishing the intrinsic values that define our humanity.
Keeping that balance may be one of our most significant challenges in the era of AI, which could encroach on our humanity if we are not truly careful.

Paris vies for Europe's AI crown
Investors pumped close to $8 billion into French tech companies in 2023, behind Britain ($13 billion) but ahead of third-place Germany ($7 billion), according to a recent report from venture capital firm Atomico. While Paris may not immediately challenge London for the top spot, tech startups have been popping up in France at a faster rate than anywhere else in Europe, with close to 3,000 founded in 2023, according to Atomico. A similar number set up shop in Britain over the same period, but the number of new companies founded there each year has been in decline since 2020.
France will this week host tech executives and political figures including former U.S. secretary of state John Kerry, EU industrial chief Thierry Breton and ex-Google boss Eric Schmidt as it looks to assert Paris' role as an AI hub.
The "Viva Technology" conference will put French innovators front-and-centre as attendees tackle key questions around artificial intelligence (AI), including its potential impact on upcoming elections and climate change.
Paris-based LVMH, the world's largest luxury group, has also thrown its weight behind VivaTech as a founding partner of the event.
Its Chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault - one of the world's wealthiest individuals - is expected to draw crowds during his visit to the group's sprawling stand, featuring new tech from prestigious brands like Louis Vuitton, Tag Heuer and Dior.
Over the past 18 months, France has attempted to build a reputation as a leader in generative AI, the technology behind OpenAI's ChatGPT and similar tools, striving to attract new startup launches.
President Emmanuel Macron has drawn investments from American big tech companies like Amazon and Microsoft, while trying to revive EU plans to better integrate capital markets across the continent. He hopes that will help to raise the capital needed to nurture emerging AI companies.
Paris' status as the global capital of luxury can help it attract investment in technology as well, organizers say.
"Luxury is always linked with innovation, because your aim is always to provide something no-one else can provide," said Francois Bitouzet, managing director of VivaTech, who cited Britain's exit from the EU as a factor in France's growth.

BUZZIEST COMPANIES
In the 18 months since ChatGPT sparked the generative AI craze, some of the most lucrative fundraising rounds have been raised by Paris-based companies.
Some of Paris' buzziest companies were founded by former researchers at industry stalwarts like Google DeepMind, such as Mistral AI and Holistic AI.
Last September, Julien Launay quit his job at Hugging Face, a leading French-American AI firm, to launch his own startup, Adaptive ML, which helps other companies build their own generative AI tools, and has staff in Paris and New York.

While the EU offers a huge single market for goods and services, capital markets in all 27 member states come with a maze of different securities laws, taxes and accounting - resulting in higher compliance costs and less liquid markets.

title: Should The Federal Government Regulate Artificial Intelligence?
text:
Artificial intelligence is in the public policy spotlight. In October 2023, the Biden Administration issued a Presidential Executive Order on AI directing federal agencies to cooperate in protecting the public from potential AI-related harms. President Biden said in his March 2024 State of the Union address that government enforcers will crack down on the use of AI to facilitate illegal price-fixing. Congress is in the preliminary stages of considering legislation that could pave the way for future regulation of AI.
The European Union went “one better” by adopting a far-reaching AI act in March 2024. It bans AI systems that are “considered to pose an unacceptable risk for the health, safety, and fundamental rights of individuals.” The act also regulates general purpose AI models that can be applied to a wide variety of tasks, imposing obligations on them according to the level of risk they impose, or are believed to impose, on the public.
Should the federal government follow in Europe’s footsteps and adopt comprehensive AI regulation to forestall bad conduct? The short answer is no, not at this time.
Laws Already On The Books Disincentivize AI Abuses
First, keep in mind that AI, like all other technologies, is already fully subject to generally applicable U.S. criminal and civil laws.
Indeed, the 2023 AI Executive Order highlighted the application of these laws (which address civil rights, national security, antitrust, privacy, labor rights, health care, and foreign affairs) to challenge the full array of potential AI abuses.
This is more than rhetoric. The Justice Department, for example, is reported to be “escalating” its antitrust probe of a criminal scheme to raise and fix rental housing prices with the use of AI algorithmic software. And in January 2024, the Federal Trade Commission announced it was investigating the competitive effects of AI-related partnerships and investments.
These and similar government initiatives send a strong signal to AI developers to avoid harmful conduct.
Regulation Is The Foe Of Innovation And Economic Growth
Case-by-case enforcement of general laws allows specific business abuses to be targeted and addressed, without otherwise interfering in business planning and initiatives.
Regulation, by contrast, establishes a framework of rules governing private sector conduct. Too often, this turns into inflexible, one-size-fits-all approaches which can ignore specific commercial circumstances and fail to respond in a timely manner to changes in technology and the business environment. Often, it’s the already-entrenched business interests which benefit by leveraging their influence and manipulating this regulation to maintain their advantages.
A statistical analysis published in 2017 in the Journal of Regulatory Economics found that more-regulated industries had fewer new firms and slower employment growth in all firms. It also noted that “[l]arge firms may even successfully lobby government officials to increase regulations to raise their smaller rivals’ costs.”
Regulation also tends to reduce innovation, as found in a 2023 American Economic Review article. Innovation is a key to higher productivity and economic growth, as explained in a 2017 European Central Bank paper.
Those factors counsel strongly against rushing to regulate a new technology which is currently is accelerating innovation in a wide range of applications and may require new governing approaches, just as the commercialization of the internet once did. Specific cases spotlight the benefits of avoiding too-much, too-soon regulation.
American Internet Freedom Versus The EU’s Stifling Approach
The U.S. decision not to overregulate the internet in its infancy is a great public policy success that public policymakers examining AI should study closely. Economic analyst Mohamed Mouti explores the fruits of this decision in EconLog:
“In the mid-1990s, the Clinton administration made a wise choice. They declared the internet a ‘market-driven area,’ not regulated, with limited government involvement only to support and enforce a predictable, minimalist, consistent, and simple legal environment. This policy allowed a new generation of creative minds to explore this frontier for business and commerce. This approach led to the internet’s success, resulting in a surge of innovation. Today, the US is home to the most innovative tech firms, hosting vibrant internet-based companies and bringing countless benefits to consumers and small businesses.”
In contrast, the European Union, which favors the “precautionary principle” of avoiding risk through early adoption of regulation, has had a terrible innovation track record.
Take the case of the EU’s efforts to regulate data privacy through its 2018 General Data Protection Regulation. GDPR requires firms to guarantee user rights related to access, consent, erasure, and data portability. There is already substantial evidence that it tends to impose high compliance costs and entrench incumbent companies, raise barriers to entry, and harm startups, entry, and smaller firms.
This history should give pause to anyone who believes that the AI Act will help position Europe to be an AI leader.
Is Now Really The Time?
Regulation is justified when its benefits can be shown to outweigh its costs. Of course, cost-benefit appraisals are imperfect and error-prone. In a famous 1969 article, the renowned economist Harold Demsetz warned against comparing an idealized version of a regulatory proposal (assuming it will work perfectly) to the actual outcomes of the current unregulated system.
The history of harmful regulatory imperfections underscores the wisdom of Demsetz’s warning. U.S. adoption of AI regulation would in all likelihood slow the rate of innovation in technology systems that appear poised to confer enormous benefits on society. Even small reductions in the AI growth rate can lead to huge long-term social welfare losses. Imagine what innovation-driven benefits might have been lost had the government decided to essentially control the internet 30 years ago.
What about AI-related harm? That is highly speculative at this point. Moreover, the federal government is closely monitoring the AI sector, ready to apply existing targeted legal sanctions at the first sign of a problem.
In sum, the AI landscape today features rapidly growing benefits and uncertain costs that, in all likelihood, can be well addressed under existing law if problems arise.
The time may (or may not) come when serious new and unanticipated AI-related problems arise that can best be handled through targeted regulatory solutions. But as of now, the case to regulate AI today has not been made.

title: Dell Technologies BrandVoice: The AI Era Needs A Fresh Approach For Cultivating Content Creation
text:
The infrastructure for fueling generative AI models and applications is underserved. But it doesn’t have to be.
Organizations face several hurdles preparing their businesses to benefit from generative AI technologies. Chief among those is preparing data and feeding it to the right models to generate valuable content and insights.
While such challenges get plenty of attention, the plumbing that helps build and nurture GenAI solutions is often overlooked and underserved. Software may still be eating the world, but infrastructure that can help organizations meet the demands of the AI era is setting the table.
Major stumbling blocks include scarcity of certain components, such as GPU chips that help fuel GenAI computations. Some organizations wait up to a one year or longer for the precious silicon.
Engineers who can connect the data pipes to the right equipment to support GenAI models, let alone train, augment or fine-tune them to fulfill business needs are also hard to hire—and harder still to retain.
These hurdles present a stark reality: most companies are behind on building the foundations to support GenAI. Yet success in the evolving global economy hinges on how quickly and effectively organizations can architect the systems capable of generating value from GenAI.
To build proper foundations for GenAI applications, it’s important to understand how the language models that fuel them function.
Data Tokens Are AI’s Critical Currency
GenAI large language models (LLMs) are trained on strings of letters, words or phrases known as data tokens, the smallest units of input that models process, and learn to predict the next token in a sequence. Each model features context windows, or the measure of how many data tokens the model can consider at any one time.
GenAI models require iterative, persistent tuning, enabling the algorithms to process large amounts of data continuously as they train and refine the models. When data goes into the models, they execute their calculations and create output.
LLMs, as well as small language models, require reliable infrastructure to support these computational processes, which become more complex as context windows grow larger.
Traditional IT infrastructures, which use traditional silicon such as CPUs, are often insufficient to handle the parallel processing AI demands.
Compounding the challenges, much of this data and applications have grown decentralized over time, running on premises, in multiple clouds and at the edge. As a result, IT departments are focusing on distributed computing approaches.
Today 82% of IT leaders prefer an on premises or hybrid approach for deploying GenAI, according to Dell research.1
Taking a Fresh Approach
To make the most of the AI boom, every business must produce repeatable results as they work to create content at scale.
That entails procuring technologies capable of providing the computational horsepower to support model inputs and outputs. It requires, for instance, organizations to pair servers with storage to fuel the best performance possible for the models that fuel GenAI applications.
Often organizations opt to bring AI close to where data resides to reduce latency, lower costs and maintain data security by keeping sensitive information within a controlled environment. Yet the path forward isn’t always clear.
Trusted partners such as Dell Technologies can help by offering technological references and tools that can serve as a beacon for organizations struggling to build AI foundations.
We call this approach the Dell AI Factory, a portfolio of products and services tailored for AI workloads and designed to achieve repeatable outcomes. The Dell AI Factory will help customers identify the AI use cases that will drive the greatest business impact and help deploy and scale GenAI applications with validated reference designs and solutions.
Dell’s professional services teams are standing by to assist organizations at every step of their GenAI journeys including helping organizations identify potential partners to work with from the open ecosystem.
Today organizations recognize that accelerating into the AI turn is a business imperative. To survive and thrive, every business must fortify their foundation.
The age of the AI factory is here.
