title: AI Might Be Smarter Than Your CMO
text:
Can artificial intelligence understand customers and predict their reactions better than human executives? The answer is “yes,” at least for some executives in some situations. An experiment I conducted using one generative AI tool, Anthropic’s Claude 3, showed the model could exhibit a surprising level of emotional intelligence. No large language model (LLM) actually “understands” emotions, but that doesn’t mean an LLM can’t be a useful check on a company’s customer interactions and communications.
AI and Jobs
Lots of jobs will be eliminated or restructured by artificial intelligence. Not long ago, pundits claimed that “nobody has lost their job to AI.” That might have been true at some point, but certainly isn’t today. Lower level jobs are the first to go. For example, Klarna recently eliminated 700 outsourced call center jobs, for example. The firm noted that AI interactions achieved similar satisfaction scores to humans, and handled tasks in two minutes vs. eleven minutes for human reps. Most notably, Klarna said switching to AI would drop an additional $40 million in profit to their bottom line.
With that kind of money at stake, every firm will be looking for similar opportunities. Offshore call centers may be the first to be impacted, but I predict the majority of the nearly three million U.S. call center jobs may be in peril in the coming years. Coding, content writing, and many other types of jobs are being affected today.
To Empathize is Human?
Conventional wisdom says that leadership roles are safe from being replaced by AI. Leaders must think strategically, be creative, and be able to both understand and connect with humans - customers, employees and other stakeholders. These are all things that AI isn’t known for.
In particular, people doubt the ability of a soulless large language model to truly understand how humans feel and react to various situations. If any part of a leadership role is impossible for code to emulate, empathy would be near the top of the list.
Steve Jobs was a difficult person, by all accounts, but he did have the ability to understand how people would react to products and features. He knew intuitively that remarkably good packaging would help customers believe in the beautiful products within. He was demanding with Apple engineers and designers because he understood the company’s customers.
Similarly, Jeff Bezos understood that customers would respond to simplicity and speed. He fought to keep One Click ordering a patented advantage, innovated with frustration-free packaging, continuously reduced delivery times, and even encouraged returns by making them nearly effortless.
Empathizing with their customers let these leaders understand their hidden desires, predict their reactions and ultimately create two of the biggest, most profitable companies on the planet.
Not All Leaders Are Great at Empathy
Here’s the catch: Jobs and Bezos were unicorns. Many business leaders at all levels struggle to understand their customers. And, even some leaders that do understand their customers fail to put the customer ahead of hitting profit targets or other goals.
Recently, I wrote about a cruise line that inconvenienced 700 of its best customers to create a mid-ocean photo opportunity with ships from sister brands. To accommodate the shoot, passengers aboard the Silversea Nova, a small luxury ship, would arrive in their final port hours late, meaning most guests would have to book new flights or make hotel arrangements. To compound the problem, this would be in the middle of Florida’s Spring Break when flights and hotels are packed with revelers.
The Nova guests were informed of the change by a letter that referred to the delay as “slight” and advised guests whose flights were impacted to adjust them. The sole recognition that redoing flights in the middle of their vacation at a time of peak travel demand might be inconvenient was an offer to reimburse “reasonable” out-of-pocket costs related to flight changes.
The letter further encouraged guests to join in a celebration on the pool deck during the photo shoot.
In my earlier article, I criticized the letter for its lack of empathy. It didn’t acknowledge the inconvenience and frustration that guests expecting a luxurious cruise and seamless experience would feel. Unsurprisingly, guests were furious and vented their anger on various cruise forums.
The decisions involved in this photo shoot were clearly made at a high level. Rerouting three ships mid-cruise, hiring a helicopter videography unit, and agreeing to reimburse extra flight expenses would require top level approval. Inexplicably, it seems that nobody expected the Nova passengers to be upset. The leaders approving this event failed to empathize with their customers.
Two Failures of Empathy
The first lack of empathy was in the decision to reroute the Nova and delay its arrival by hours. Someone decided that the marketing assets generated from the photoshoot would be of enough value to offset the considerable costs involved. They also decided that the inconvenience to the Nova passengers would be of minor importance. They clearly didn’t put themselves in the position of a guest who had booked their perfect flight months earlier who would now have to scramble for whatever flights and seats might be available at the last minute.
The second failure of empathy was in the letter that communicated the change to the Nova guests. It didn’t apologize. It didn’t even mention the inconvenience and extra effort the guests would experience. The tone was purely transactional. The cruise line offered to reimburse out-of-pocket costs (if they were “reasonable”), as if this was merely about money.
It’s possible that an empathetic leader could have decided that the marketing assets were indeed incredibly valuable and unobtainable in any other way. But, that truly empathetic leader would have communicated with the affected guests in a totally different way.
Can AI Be Empathetic?
I conducted a simple experiment to see if AI could outperform the cruise line executives responsible for the photoshoot episode in predicting customer reactions and communicating the change to affected guests. That’s not a high bar, to be sure, but I was unexpectedly impressed by the apparent emotional intelligence demonstrated by Claude 3, the AI LLM I tested.
I’m not going to claim that Claude or any other AI truly “understands” human emotions. But those who dismiss generative AI as mere “predictors of the next word” miss the point that it can be a useful tool for leaders, marketers, and anyone trying to predict customer reactions and communicate skillfully.
Claude 3 Analyzes the Letter
In the interest of brevity, I’m not going to include the full text of prompts and responses here. I first asked Claude 3 Sonnet (the free version) to rate the letter Nova guests received for empathy and predict how they might react. I was cautious not to prime Claude in any way, only adding timing details the context that the Nova was a luxury “five star” cruise ship that attracted guests who tended to be older, wealthier, and more frequent cruisers.
Here are a few salient points from Claude’s analysis:
2 out of 5 for Empathy. Claude rated the letter as a “2” on a scale of 5 for empathy. It notes that while the letter “attempts to explain the situation and offer solutions, it lacks genuine empathy and consideration for the impact on the guests' experiences.”
Impersonal Tone. Claude accurately describes the tone of the letter as “formal and impersonal,” and says, “It fails to acknowledge the significant disruption and potential stress caused by a 4-hour delay, especially for guests on a luxury cruise expecting a seamless experience.”
No Extra Compensation. Claude pointed out that the letter failed to offer “any compensation or gesture of goodwill to the guests, beyond reimbursing travel change fees.”
Tone Deaf. Claude didn’t like framing the photo shoot as a “celebration” and thought the “request for guests to gather on the pool deck and ‘toast together’ comes across as tone-deaf.”
Am I the only one who finds it amusing when an AI calls a human “tone-deaf?”
Predicted Reaction from Guests
One to evaluate empathy skills is to see how well someone can predict the reaction of other people to a particular stimulus. In this example, either the cruise line leaders failed to predict how guests would feel, or, even worse, didn’t care.
Negative reactions. Claude correctly predicted that “many guests will react negatively to this letter.” I described some of their reactions in my earlier article. It pointed out that these luxury ship guests, “have high expectations and pay a premium for exceptional service and a seamless experience.”
Prioritizing Marketing. Claude’s next comment nailed it: There would be a “perception of prioritizing marketing over guest experience.” I might have used the word “demonstration” instead of “perception” - there’s zero doubt that in this case creating marketing assets trumped customer experience.
I didn’t tell Claude that Silversea’s “Credo” begins with, “We make the satisfaction of our guests our first priority...” I have little doubt that had I done so it would have pointed out the contradiction, if not the irony.
Dissatisfaction with Communication. Claude accurately predicted the impersonal tone of the letter and failure to acknowledge the inconvenience would lead “guests to feel that their concerns and experiences are not being prioritized or handled appropriately.”
Negative Word Of Mouth. Claude noted, “Disgruntled guests on a luxury cruise are likely to share their negative experiences with others...” This is exactly what happened in various Facebook groups and the huge forum, Cruise Critic.
Recommendations. Claude closed with an unsolicited plan of action: “...it would be advisable for the cruise line to take a more empathetic and proactive approach. This could include a sincere apology, personalized communication and support, generous compensation or future cruise credits, and a clear prioritization of the guest experience over marketing opportunities.”
That advice sounds like what an in-touch leader or customer experience expert would suggest.
Damage Control
I gave Claude one final prompt. I explained that the letter had been sent, and asked it to draft a new letter to try to limit the damage from the first one. The letter it drafted is the letter that passengers should have received in the first place:
“On behalf of the entire Deluxe Cruises family, I want to extend my sincere apologies for the significant inconvenience... you have placed your trust in us to provide an exceptional and seamless experience, and we have fallen short in this instance...
We deeply regret the disruption this will create to your travel plans and the stress it may cause.”
The letter outlined specific actions, indeed the very actions the cruise line should have promised in the first place. Here are some excerpts:
“1. Our dedicated Guest Experience team will be reaching out to each of you individually to understand your specific travel arrangements and provide personalized assistance in modifying any necessary reservations, including flights, ground transportation, and accommodations.
2. We will gladly cover any reasonable change fees, cancellation costs, or fare differences associated with adjusting your travel plans...
3. As a gesture of goodwill and to express our sincere regret for this inconvenience, we will be providing... a future cruise credit valued at 25% of your current voyage fare...
4. For those guests who may have non-refundable arrangements or commitments that cannot be easily adjusted, we will be offering complimentary one-night hotel accommodations in Fort Lauderdale...”
The letter went on to offer additional reassurance:
“...We will have additional staff and resources on hand to assist you upon arrival... and I encourage you to reach out to any member of our team should you require further support or have any special needs.”
Claude’s letter finished with another apology and a promise to do better in the future. Clearly, the letter was written without knowledge of what resources would be available. Perhaps an open-ended commitment on costs or future cruise credit would be unreasonably expensive. Nevertheless, the letter addresses the guest pain points - if all of the proposed actions seem too costly, then perhaps the photoshoot was a bad idea.
Can AI Replace Your CMO?
We’re a long way from AI replacing humans in senior leadership roles. But, there are countless ways AI can make these humans more successful. Based on the cruise photoshoot episode, here are two ways generative AI can be used to drive better outcomes:
- Describe a situation or proposed change and ask how customers will react. Companies often make changes or take actions only to realize they had misjudged how customers would react. Surveys or focus groups could help, but if time and/or money preclude these options, AI can step in with no incremental cost. Detailed descriptions of the customers and the situation will stimulate more relevant answers. In many cases, the predictions will match those of the people making the decision. In some cases, they may be wrong. But getting a second opinion never hurts.
- Ask AI to review and redraft customer communications. Claude’s “damage control” letter was far more empathetic that the initial notification sent to the ship’s guests. The draft AI creates shouldn’t be the final one, but it will provide a starting point for a communication that hits all the right notes. This process should build on the details used in the first step - the better the model understands the customers, the situation, and the intent of the communication, the better the result will be.
It’s important to note that my experiment used a public LLM with prompts of minimal complexity. A custom model, or even a public model that has digested a lot of your company’s content, will yield more relevant results.
At least for now, don’t assume your AI model is providing accurate, or even truthful, answers. Double check when appropriate, and use caution when acting on recommendations. Consider your AI model to be a helpful but somewhat inexperienced associate that is great for generating ideas and for acting as a sounding board.
AI won’t replace your CMO, but it may make your CMO better.

title: How AI Admissions Recruiters Will Transform Enrollment
text:
AI admissions recruiters are here, and they are poised to completely transform enrollment management forever.
Starting this summer, AI recruiters will go out into the world, pair 1-1 with an institution’s prospective students and personally nurture them across email, SMS, direct mail, and even phone calls to drive applications. The rise of the AI recruiter represents a new epoch for strategic enrollment management — one that promises to transform and improve the college process for students, parents, admissions officers, and enrollment leaders.
Once they are widely deployed, AI recruiters will raise the bar for college marketing and communications, offer the first viable solution to the admissions staffing crisis, and dismantle critical enrollment barriers for parents and students.
The quality standards for effective institutional marketing and communications are about to rise irrevocably
AI recruiters will completely transform how students and parents experience the prospect and inquiry stages of an institutional funnel.
Today, the default student experience at the top of the funnel trends towards a basic email journey, perhaps with a couple of branches within a larger drip campaign. “Personalization” in this world might mean inserting a first name into an email subject line or swapping out the name of a major on a student postcard. Anything more individualized usually has to wait until a student has applied and been admitted — after which colleges ramp up the level of personal engagement and staff involvement.
The recruitment process has had to work this way up until 2024 because of the sheer size of university funnels. When you have 50,000, 100,000, or 250,000 prospects in your CRM and 15–25 staff members, you can’t realistically do anything more personalized than mass marketing email campaigns. It’s simply not feasible to give every student extended personal attention. This capacity mismatch has driven many universities to partner with search marketing firms such as EAB and RNL, but those firms also have real human staffing constraints. The net result is outsourced marketing emails that look eerily similar to those of your main competitors
With AI recruiters, however, every single interaction a student has with an institution will be 100% personalized to them and them alone — their experience of the admissions process will feel like working one-on-one with a member of staff. Every email, text, postcard, or brochure will be completely tailored to the student’s needs, future goals, and college preferences.
AI recruiters can even hold full-fledged phone conversations with students, and these aren’t the same as the automated tree systems you’ve experienced when calling your bank or airline (no student will ever hear “press 0 to speak with a representative.”) Instead, students can have an intelligent, dynamic 15-minute conversation about a college with an AI recruiter, or get continuous one-on-one support while filling out their application or wrangling the FAFSA.
AI recruiters ultimately answer the question: how would you interact with each student in your CRM if you had another 1,000 admissions officers on staff? For most colleges, this holds the potential to completely reverse years of declining student engagement and funnel performance.
The flip side of this is that the quality bar for college marketing is about to go way up, creating a major risk for schools who don’t have an AI recruiter.
This is what a standard marketing email might look like in a student inbox.
Meanwhile, this is what an email from an AI recruiter might look like.
Which of these emails is a prospective student more likely to engage with?
At the end of the day, student inboxes are really noisy. The median junior receives more than 1,500 college emails in their inbox each year, and it’s no surprise that they ignore or bounce from the vast majority of them. Personal emails from an AI recruiter will finally have a chance to cut through the noise. And AI recruiters aren't constrained to email, although their emails will be magnitudes better - they'll also learn student open and click behavior and use it to follow up smartly via phone call, text, and more.
AI recruiters may finally offer a real solution to the enrollment staffing crisis
Admissions offices are facing a staffing crisis. Enrollment teams are struggling with up to 50% turnover and as many as 2/3 of admissions officers reported feelings of burnout in the past year. Training and hiring new staff members is also incredibly expensive (both in terms of time and money), and office operations and processes are incredibly brittle. If you polled enrollment leaders at the 2,000+ four-year colleges and universities in the United States, they would uniformly call out staffing and operational capacity as one of their top three challenges.
AI recruiters may be the solution. Once deployed, a trained AI recruiter adds the capabilities of 1,000 well-trained new hires simultaneously to the team, working to create better results from the top to the middle of an institutional funnel.
At the same time, AI recruiters are not a replacement for human admissions officers; instead, they free up those humans to spend time on the highest impact student engagements. AI recruiters scale 1-1 guidance at the top of a college’s funnel so that the team can focus mainly on engaging directly with students at the admit stage. Tripling down on efforts there increases the value of the entire team’s time, while positively impacting yield rates.
Human admissions officers will also play a critical role in navigating complex student scenarios and dealing with edge cases. And they already have to prioritize their time in this way today. The difference is that in a world with AI recruiters, students will be handed off to work with admissions officers having had a much better experience at the top of the funnel, with much more affinity for the institution as a result.
AI recruiters will remove barriers for students and parents
AI recruiters will create a lot of value for institutions, but they will also be better for students and their families. In particular, they will break down a series of enrollment barriers that currently hamper student progression throughout the admissions process.
Perhaps the biggest lift will come from 24/7 availability. During the traditional workday, students are in school and many parents are working. Most college exploration for families happens in the evening and on weekends. With an AI recruiter, that 9 pm email will instead get an instantaneous response. Someone is always available to take a call on Saturday afternoon, and offices will have enough capacity to handle 1,000 simultaneous student questions on the night of the application deadline.
For institutions that serve diverse student populations, AI recruiters will also offer transformative linguistic capabilities. Especially in households where English isn’t the first language for parents, AI recruiters will enable enrollment teams to have fluent, real-time conversations in more than 30 languages including Spanish, Arabic, French, Vietnamese, and more.
Lastly, AI recruiters will give offices the capacity to simultaneously assist thousands of students in navigating through any enrollment barrier, whether that’s filling out the application, navigating financial aid, or understanding how their community college courses map as credit into degree programs.
By raising the baseline for admissions and enrollment management, AI recruiters are set to revolutionize the college recruitment process, making it more efficient and personalized for colleges, and more accessible for students and parents.

title: UAE and US to seal more AI deals: UAE minister - ET Telecom
text:

UAE and US to seal more AI deals: UAE minister
The stakes have risen as neighbouring Saudi Arabia has begun pitching itself as a prospective hub for AI activity outside the United States.
By Federico Maccioni
DUBAI: The United Arab Emirates and United States will invest more in artificial intelligence as part of a strategic partnership, the UAE's state minister for AI Omar Sultan Al Olama said on Tuesday.
The UAE, led by government-backed firm G42, is striving to become a global leader in AI, invested heavily in it to help the Gulf nation diversify away from oil.
The stakes have risen as neighbouring Saudi Arabia has begun pitching itself as a prospective hub for AI activity outside the United States.
"In terms of our investments, since the U.S. is now considering the UAE as a strategic partner, and the UAE is reciprocating that by considering the U.S. as a strategic partner, you will see more deals naturally," Al Olama told Reuters on the sidelines of an event in Dubai.
Microsoft is investing $1.5 billion in G42, the two companies announced last month, giving the U.S. giant a minority stake and a board seat and allowing the two to deepen ties.
As part of the deal, which the two companies said was backed by assurances to the U.S. and UAE governments over security, G42 would use Microsoft cloud services to run its AI applications.
That partnership comes amid Washington's efforts to hobble Beijing's technological advances, with the United States adding four Chinese companies to an exports blacklist for seeking to acquire AI chips for China's military.
Asked about further potential divestment of Chinese tech companies by the UAE, Al Olama said "government-to-government the UAE is a neutral country, and in that sense, we are going to be a country that allows the world to do business in the UAE".
Al Olama said a diversified energy mix, including nuclear energy, was key for attracting AI investment to the tiny Gulf country.
"We will have the ability to expand our energy infrastructure based on the need of the data centres," the minister said.
This includes discussions about small modular nuclear reactors but there were no concrete plans yet, he said.
The UAE has operated a South Korean-built nuclear plant since 2021. The country plans to also tender as soon as this year for four more nuclear reactors, Reuters reported last month, citing three sources.
On Tuesday, French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire flagged during a visit to Abu Dhabi that Paris was open to the UAE investing in its nuclear energy industry. He also said he the two countries would sign a strategic partnership on AI.

title: Nutanix Cements Enterprise AI Foundations With GPT-In-A-Box 2.0
text:
AI is double-ended. Most users’ exposure levels to AI services comes in the form of upper-level chatbot interfaces, automated smart application functions or the AI found in the new breed of generative Artificial Intelligence (gen-AI) tools such as Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini and of course ChatGPT. Equally, as one would expect, a good deal of AI engineering happens at the back-end with the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), proprietary enterprise data model extensions and the infrastructure and platform engineering layers needed to make these often-weighty cloud-based application tiers work.
Because AI itself is still at an essentially embryonic experimental layer, firms are seeking ways to elevate their enterprise applications with this new intelligence; this in turn means their primary interest is on user-level AI and how to apply automated services for better business outcomes.
Less appealing perhaps, are the tasks associated with building the back-end of AI.
The inference difference
Hybrid multi-cloud company Nutanix says it has recognized this trend and is now extending its Nutanix GPT-in-a-Box technology, including integrations with Nvidia NIM inference microservices and the Hugging Face Large Language Models (LLMs) library. Nvidia Inference Microservices (NIM) provides access to community-built AI models via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) optimized and accelerated by the company’s own Graphical Processing Units (GPUs).
"We saw a great response to our original launch of Nutanix GPT-in-a-Box [in summer 2023], validating the needs of enterprise customers for on-premises software solutions that simplify the deployment and management of AI models and inference endpoints,” said Thomas Cornely, SVP of product management at Nutanix.
This technology is a software-defined AI-ready platform and services offering that helps size and configure hardware and software infrastructure suitable to deploy a curated set of Large Language Models (LLMs) using the open source AI and MLOps (machine learning operations) frameworks on the Nutanix Cloud Platform. Nutanix GPT-in-a-Box is a full stack solution (everything from operating system to database to application services is included) built to simplify enterprise AI adoption with tight integration with Nutanix Objects and Nutanix Files for model and data storage.
Version 2.0
Cornely has now drawn attention to the launch of GPT-in-a-Box 2.0, which has been built to to deliver expanded Nvidia accelerated computing and LLM support. It also offers simplified foundational model management (foundation models being the base layer knowledge pools used to create and develop ‘narrow’ specific AI services from) and integrations with Nvidia NIMs microservices and the Hugging Face LLM library. GPT-in-a-Box 2.0 will include a unified user interface for foundation model management, API endpoint creation, end user access key management and Nvidia Tensor Core GPUs.
According to Cornely and team, “GPT-in-a-Box 2.0 will bring Nutanix simplicity to the user experience with a built-in Graphical User Interface, role-based access control, auditability and dark site support [on-premises deployments without a web connection, such as defense], among other benefits.”
If we’re interested in the ability to configure infrastructure layers for AI in simpler ways so that enterprises can actually work on crafting and grafting AI into their apps, then that’s what we’re seeing here. That is to say, this service will provide a point-and-click-user interface to deploy and configure Nvidia NIM, part of the Nvidia AI enterprise software platform for the development and deployment of production-grade AI, to easily deploy and run gen-AI workloads in the enterprise and at the computing edge.
Unstructured data platform for AI/ML
“Nutanix also enhanced its unstructured data platform for AI/ML and other applications with increased performance, density and Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). Nutanix Unified Storage (NUS) now supports a new 550+ terabytes dense low-cost all-NVMe platform and up to 10 Gigabyte/second sequential read throughput from a single node (close to line speed for a 100 Gigabit ethernet port) enabling faster data reads and more efficient use of GPU resources. Additionally, to protect the valuable and often confidential data such as datasets used to train and process AI/ML workloads, Nutanix Data Lens extends cyber resilience value to Objects in addition to Files data,” noted the company, in a technical statement.
To support customers’ AI strategies, Nutanix announced the new AI Partner Program providing customers with simplified access to an expanded ecosystem of AI partners to deliver real-world GenAI solutions.
As noted, Nutanix also announced a partnership with Hugging Face to provide access to the Hugging Face library and execution of Large Language Models (LLMs). This means AI app developers can use Nutanix GPT-in-a-Box 2.0 to consume validated LLMs from Hugging Face and execute them.
Through this partnership, Nutanix and Hugging Face will develop a custom integration with Text Generation Inference, a Hugging Face open source library for production deployment of Large Language Models and enable text-generation models available on the Hugging Face Hub within Nutanix GPT-in-a-Box 2.0. It will deliver a usable workflow to deploy validated AI LLMs from Hugging Face with support from Nutanix. This is said to create a jointly validated and supported workflow for Hugging Face libraries and LLMs to give users a single point of management for consistent model inference.
“Our partnership with Nutanix will help extend Hugging Face to more enterprises looking for private and secure control of their LLMs,” said Clem Delangue, CEO and co-founder, Hugging Face. “Our mission is to enable organizations of all sizes to build their own AI with open source. Our work with Nutanix will make it easy for enterprises to build AI applications on-premises leveraging Text Generation Inference.”
The road to better AI infrastructure
What we're seeing here is point-and-click AI infrastructure. What we’re seeing here is validated LLM consumption. What we’re also seeing here is the so-called single-pane-of-glass management layer that the IT industry loves to talk about as platform providers try to remove the need for software engineers to move between toolsets, libraries and even data sources in ways that could introduce errors.
Given that removing errors from our new AI services and eradicating bias and AI hallucinations is of paramount interest, these could be helpful developments. Slicker AI infrastructure might also be argued to produce more efficient code and - in a world that now thankfully champions green coding sustainability - this is also a good thing.
“The Broadcom acquisition [of VMware] is creating a major storm in terms of disruptive risks, but what I can tell you is that we are here to help you navigate the storm. What I can tell you about Nutanix is that we are an engineering company - and we work to put consumer-like simplicity into the enterprise while also delivering Total Cost of Ownership benefits,” said Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami. “When we look at building state of the art hybrid cloud and modernizing infrastructure to enable the roll-out of AI, we have been working to make sure our technology has freedom of choice built in. If you look at where we are today, we are an infrastructure software company - but that’s not where we want to be tomorrow… if you look at the future, it’s about being a platform for modern applications with the capability to work with cloud-native technologies in containers.”
This decade’s AI renaissance has been as chaotic as it has been inspirational, invigorating and innovation-fuelled i.e. organizations have had to think about the back-end infrastructure, the front-end user interface, the data layer in between and the wider social impact of AI apps and how they affect peoples’ roles in the workplace. Add those responsibilities to the need to cost-manage cloud-based AI using FinOps principles, plus the requirements organizations need to think about to meet regulatory compliance pressures… and many would agree that the path to better AI infrastructure is worth travelling.
Has Nutanix fixed this journey in its entirety? It’s unlikely, there will be further potholes and cracks to fix on the way, at least we know the cement mixer is now running.

title: The AI PC Revolution Is About To Get Real With Copilot+
text:
Just ahead of Microsoft’s Build conference that’s happening in Seattle today, the company kicked off a big, new campaign called the Copilot+ PC. Along with major ecosystem partners like Qualcomm, Intel and AMD, and big-name OEM partners like Dell, HP, Lenovo and Samsung, Microsoft better defined the hardware requirements and expected experiences from the modern AI-powered PC, and it goes far beyond just a Neural Processing Unit-equipped machine capable of at least 40 TOPS. In fact, the Redmond company detailed Windows PC experiences that will be “20x more powerful and up to 100x as efficient for running AI workloads and deliver industry-leading AI acceleration,” in addition to “outperforming Apple’s MacBook Air 15” by up to 58% in sustained multithreaded performance, all while delivering all-day battery life.” These are bold promises to be sure, but again, the full might of the PC ecosystem is behind this initiative, with new cutting-edge silicon in support of it as well, starting with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite and X Plus platforms.
Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite And X Plus Mop-Up Major PC Design Wins
If there ever was a show of force for a new entrant in the PC space, it would have to have been Qualcomm’s proverbial parade of Snapdragon PC design wins and Microsoft’s strong backing (which is not easy to garner) of the new, fully custom Arm-based platform. In recent months, Qualcomm had been teasing its next generation Snapdragon X Elite and X Plus series of processors, making stark performance claims versus both X86 incumbents, as well as MacBooks. And it appears, based on what looks like very enthusiastic adoption by major PC OEMs, those claims should be well-founded. In fact, I can’t recall an all-new, competitive mobile PC platform launch that’s had this much inertia behind it.
For example, Dell introduced a new XPS 13 laptop product (as well as Inspirons and total of 5 SKUs) based on Snapdragon X Elite, and that’s a model-brand combination that has always been an Intel-only affair. Lenovo also stepped up with the ThinkPad T14 and Yoga Slim 7x and HP launched its EliteBook Ultra and OmniBook X laptops as well. In fact, there were a plethora (over 20 devices) of Snapdragon X-powered laptops announced, from Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop 13, 15 and Pro, to Acer, ASUS, and even Samsung Galaxy Book4 Edge offerings. Qualcomm was able to win design with virtually all the major OEM players, with prominent model offerings to boot, not just some random one-off SKUs at Best Buy.
On the software and ecosystem enablement side of things, Microsoft highlighted applications such as Office 365, Adobe, Davinci Resolve Studio, Capcut, Caphable, LiquidTextd, and djay Pro will all be utilizing new AI-infused Snapdragon X Elite and X Plus capabilities to improve user productivity and foster creativity. For its part, Microsoft also unveiled a new emulator called Prism, that it claims will allow apps to run “great” under emulation, in the event an app isn’t native to Windows on Arm devices.
The bottom line is, you could say that Qualcomm scored a bit of an exclusive in Micosoft’s Copilot+ PC launch, as Snapdragon X-powered PCs were the cornerstone of the entire show. And for that, you can absolutely color me impressed.
Intel’s Lunar Lake, AMD And NVIDIA Will Weigh In
Of course, Intel likely saw all of this coming and prepared some additional messaging on its forthcoming Lunar Lake Core Ultra processor platform, which is expected to be a major lift over current gen Meteor Lake Core Ultra processors as well. Though Lunar Lake isn’t quite ready for prime time yet, it’s on track for Q3 this year (I suspect late Q3 for a Q4 shopping season ramp), and claims of Lunar Lake performance are also lofty. Specifically, Intel is projecting up to 1.5X better graphics performance from Lunar Lake’s Battlemage integrated GPU, along with faster than Snapdragon X Elite and AMD Ryzen 8000 series CPU performance. The company is also claiming up to 1.4X AI performance lift over Snapdragon X Elite in Stable Diffusion 15-based generative AI workloads, along with over 100 total platform TOPS between its GPU, NPU and CPU cores combined.
Proof points and 3rd party benchmark results will be critical for Intel’s Lunar Lake, once retail systems hit the market. However, there’s little question, based on what I’ve heard from execs at the company, that Intel is more than confident in how it will measure up versus Qualcomm and AMD both.
Speaking of which, in the next couple of weeks, around the Computex time frame, I expect we’ll hear more from AMD as well, with respect to its forthcoming Strix Point Zen 5 CPU line-up. It’s going to be a very busy Q4 for the PC industry, and NVIDIA will be chiming in to remind folks that, regardless of all these power-efficient AI PC platforms, real heavy duty local AI PC workloads will still be accelerated on powerful discrete GPUs like its GeForce RTX 40 series offering.
NVIDIA’s logic stands to reason as well, when you consider the fastest PC GPUs offer up to 1300 TOPS of AI acceleration throughput, along with a huge install base of both desktop and laptop PCs already in market. It’s hard to argue with that logic, though certainly laptops and other low power PC platforms can’t always support the power budget of a discrete GPU, along with its impact on battery life.
The AI PC Is Coming In Hot
All of this momentum, not only in terms of the completely disruptive nature of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X series, but also the intense focus of virtually all the major silicon players in modern computing and the software ecosystem that will power it, means that while the “AI PC” use to be just casual buzz words, the market is truly beginning to take shape. This new category of devices is coming clearly into focus, with features, performance, capabilities and experiential expectations that are becoming much more specifically defined. In fact, I’d dare say we’re lining up for a true inflection point in personal computing, and sooner than perhaps some projected.
The bottom line is that PCs will become more useful to us then ever before, and while it will take a bit of time for some mainstream users to come up the curve on how to harness these capabilities, this new beginning is upon us. Like so many other major markets, AI is breathing much-needed new life into the legacy personal computing experience.

title: How Love, Forgiveness & Compassion Maximize AI Project Decision Value
text:
Maximum AI value will be unlocked when humans and AI work together, not by automating people out of the loop. “There is far more opportunity in augmenting humans to do new tasks rather than automating what they can already do,” explained economist Erik Brynjolfsson in his seminal paper, The Turing Trap: The Promise & Peril of Human-Like Artificial Intelligence. Gartner analyst David Pidsley suggests this framing, “Think of [AI] as a digital counterpart, collaborating with humans to make informed and intelligent choices, leading to optimal outcomes.”
These ideas counter the common business approach of using technology to automate away human costs. After years of implementing AI as co-founder of the Cloverpop decision intelligence platform, I’ve come across many frameworks for prioritizing AI initiatives using traditional business measures like return on investment, time to market, technical feasibility and business risk. However, all of these frameworks lack a filtering step to reveal projects that meaningfully augment human capabilities.
To bridge that gap, I propose an intuitive and radically human-centric framework for making decisions about AI projects using shared human values of love, forgiveness and compassion. We can apply this framework to AI projects by asking three questions:
- Will this harm feelings of love, forgiveness and compassion? Obvious harms like physical injuries or financial losses should already place hard limits on our business initiatives. Transformative AI projects must also consider damage to feelings of love, forgiveness and compassion at the heart of our humanity.
- Will this increase feelings of love, forgiveness and compassion? People thrive when given opportunities to love, give and receive forgiveness and feel compassion. We should invest where AI creates opportunities for us to flourish.
- Will this engage feelings of love, forgiveness and compassion to drive business performance? These human emotions are unmatched motivators for rapid positive change in ourselves, our employees, our businesses and society. We should not automate these motivations out of our organizations.
While these values are foreign to AI, they are inherent to people, so this framework surfaces projects that maximally align with human values and culls those that do not. Eliminating low-value automation projects reduces substantial downside risk. Highlighting opportunities to augment humans with AI will unlock the greatest business value.
As an acid test, imagine these two stories in the press:
- “Company X disregarded love, forgiveness and compassion when selecting AI projects. Here’s what happened.”
- “Company Y emphasized love, forgiveness and compassion when selecting AI projects. Here’s what happened.”
The first story warns of AI’s dystopian downside, while the second promises true AI innovation. So, let’s consider specific examples of how we might use love, forgiveness and compassion when deciding on AI initiatives.
Love
Using AI tools to help us do our jobs and improve our lives is an enormous productivity opportunity. However, there is a slippery slope between using AI to clean up a thoughtful employee review and writing a deceptively convincing review based on a few words dashed out by a manager in the minute before their next meeting. We must be careful.
Authenticity matters when love is required, including love for employees, customers and other stakeholders, even competitors and regulators. We all know what love is. Pragmatically, humans must remain in the loop when love is involved.
For example, we should take extraordinary care before using AI to:
- Write final performance reviews or other employee or recruiting communications, from get-well and birthday messages to performance feedback, promotions, hiring and firing notices, recruiting outreach and networking.
- Manage critical customer relationship touch-points from lead nurturing and sales funnel interactions to targeted social media outreach.
- Prepare documentation relevant to regulatory reviews, especially regarding any controls pertinent to physical, mental or financial safety.
Instead, we can look for ways AI can help provide more loving experiences, products and services. For example, we can use AI to:
- Help employees wade through their floods of automated emails and messages, perform complex data analyses, identify unnecessary work and otherwise reduce unloving drudgery to leave more time for productivity, connection and creativity.
- Answer routine customer questions quickly, including direct escalation routes to efficient human-to-human conversations.
- Review complex regulatory documentation to ensure completeness, accuracy and compliance to improve human safety.
Using AI to unlock human creativity, connect people to help and improve safety are loving strategies. How often do we have a chance to bring more love into our companies? Let’s seize the opportunity AI gives us.
Forgiveness
Automating situations that are likely to require human forgiveness dehumanizes us. We cannot forgive a driverless car that kills a pedestrian because the vehicle cannot receive forgiveness – our forgiveness does not affect it. Automated harm lessens us because of this missing reciprocity.
We must avoid using AI to control areas of our businesses where forgiveness reigns. In a negative sense, it is inauthentic for AI to ask for and receive forgiveness when it has no human standing and cannot correct itself or make amends. In a positive sense, wanting and receiving forgiveness is a powerful individual and organizational motivator to drive change. Thus, when automation distances us from our mistakes or numbs our feelings, it destroys the business benefits of forgiveness. This prescription includes forgiveness for mistakes or personal harm by employees, customers, organizations and all stakeholders.
For instance, we must be cautious before using AI to:
- Mediate significant employee performance interventions or disciplinary actions, such as missed quarterly goals or workplace policy violations.
- Manage automatic refunds or apologies for egregious mistakes or misconduct, thereby blunting our visceral feelings of the need for forgiveness that would otherwise motivate rapid operational improvements.
- Deploy automated social media campaigns to downplay past harm or future risks for which we may someday seek forgiveness.
Instead, let’s look for ways AI can make forgiveness faster and easier. For example, we can use AI to:
- Analyze employee performance to identify people who may have been under or over-compensated. Then, give that information to managers so they can have heart-to-heart conversations and ask for grace when needed.
- Comb through historical customer interaction databases to detect mistakes, create lists of customers whose forgiveness we need, and help our employees send those personal apologies with maximum efficiency.
- Monitor social media for opportunities to address our mistakes with personal apologies, including tools and processes to help employees do so authentically and efficiently.
Forgiveness benefits the forgiver and the forgiven. If we care to help our employees, customers and broader society, we can give them no greater gift and receive no greater motivation for positive change.
Compassion
AI hides inhuman complexity beneath deceptively simple faux-human exteriors. Yet, despite its mind-boggling complexity, there is no ghost in the machine. If those ghosts were real, they could feel our pain and wish for solace. Machines cannot.
We will thrive by avoiding AI control of situations where compassion is necessary. Our ability to perceive suffering and our desire to relieve it is the essence of human dignity. We must not separate our awareness of suffering from our desire to give relief. In practical terms, compassion combines love and forgiveness, and delivers the business benefits of both.
So, AI should not have a controlling seat at the table when we:
- Create lists of people who need performance correction or firing without providing transparent and traceable detailed explanations of why they were selected.
- Handle the most stressful and challenging customer interactions, from escalation paths in contact centers to patient interactions in medical settings.
- Calculate return on investment, budgeting or staffing for programs intended to benefit society, thus requiring compassionate judgment.
Instead, we can use AI to dignify our companies by making it safer and easier for us to feel compassion. For example, we can use AI to:
- Assign employee mentors who are most likely to empathize with and want to support their mentees.
- Identify stress signals in customer interactions and connect frustrated, angry or despairing people with employees or even other customers who feel their pain and have the desire and ability to help relieve it.
- Sift through the flood of human suffering on social media to find ways our offerings are causing pain and bring the most compelling stories to executives to kindle compassion in our hearts and positive action in our companies.
AI cannot be compassionate. But it can help unleash compassion that often lies dormant in our companies.
The Dark Side and the Light
Love, forgiveness and compassion are the foundation of human experience. Our businesses take on dangerous downside risks and miss enormous opportunities to create value if we ignore these precious human values in the race to implement AI.
We must not diminish ourselves by allowing AI to curtail our feelings of love, forgiveness and compassion, and we must protect ourselves against the dehumanization of AI-created harm. We can thrive by using AI to unlock more opportunities to love, forgive, and be compassionate through AI projects that align with those human values. Finally, we must “never let a good crisis go to waste.” Business situations that involve love, forgiveness and compassion represent powerful engines of positive change. Let’s fuel business growth by elevating human capabilities with the power of AI.

title: Council Post: Generative AI—Going Beyond The Content
text:
Alastair is Co-Founder of Digital Marketing Agency Optix Solutions in the U.K.
Most marketers are now happy to use AI for content creation but are struggling to go beyond that. It’s here to stay, so we need to work out how to make the most of it—to create efficiency and free up capacity. To do this, there’s an element of behavioral change required.
Most of us will think of accessible AI as something relatively new, with ChatGPT available for less than two years. But I realized my journey with AI started in the late 1990s when I was a student at the University of Exeter. I recently read a course textbook by one of my tutors, Professor Derek Partridge, A New Guide to Artificial Intelligence, in which he spoke of what could be achieved when we had machines that were powerful enough.
Well, we certainly have those now, and I'm extremely proud to have taken the baton and recently authored my first e-book (link will download a free PDF) in the space of generative AI for marketing, calling it "10 Prompts That Will Transform Your Marketing Team," aimed at marketing professionals who want to improve their prompting skills.
A Brief Summary Of The Different Types Of AI
I always think it’s helpful to position what we’re hearing and reading about in the news in the context of the broader term AI. It all tends to morph into each other if we don’t. There are three main categories.
• ANI (Artificial Narrow Intelligence): It only does one thing: think Alexa or Deep Blue.
• AGI (Artificial General Intelligence): It can learn any intellectual task humans can perform.
• ASI (Artificial Superintelligence): It's self-aware. Think Skynet—the scary one!
For us, ANI—which includes ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini—is the generative version, which is rapidly becoming part of daily life for marketers. Why?
It completes long tasks in seconds, billions of data points and research pieces are at your fingertips and it helps get past creative blocks.
And this is just the tip of the iceberg.
There’s been a lot of concern that AI is going to make everyone redundant, but people are still needed to develop, train and use AI.
That’s the nub. We need to become "masters of the machine." We have to understand how to use AI brilliantly. We must become the best "prompt engineers" we can. All this means is we need to get good at extracting the best answers we can by inputting the best questions (prompts).
Caution Required
There are areas to be aware of at this still-unclear stage.
First, privacy is crucial, demanding compliance with secure AI tools. Verification of facts is also essential due to potential inaccuracies in AI-generated information. If AI tells you Tolkien wrote the Harry Potter books, would you believe it? AI is improving every day, but check, check, check. Finally, guard against bias. Because AI tools train on a variety of sources, from Wikipedia to books, it can absorb the bias and push it back to the user.
AI In Daily Life
So, let's move on to the positives of using AI as a part of your daily working life. Here are a few use cases.
• AI As Another Member Of Your Team: It can be available on your browser/phone all day.
• AI As Your Coach: It can help you to be better as a leader and person.
• AI As Your PA: It can write documents and learn agendas.
• AI As Your Friend: Maybe this feels a bit weird or far-fetched at the moment, but this may become a reality for our children.
What The Future Holds
Where do I think it’s going? The next stage in generative AI for marketers is likely to be customization—creating your own unique GPTs (if you’re using ChatGPT or variants with others). With these customizations, you could have GPTs for:
• Branding support, providing you with assets that take account of your company's brand guidelines.
• Onboarding partner, a crucial part of the recruitment and onboarding process.
• Budgeting associate, strategizing your annual budget.
• Content creation, taking into account your company's values and tone of voice.
And so much more.
Going back to the nub of this, I believe what’s critical for marketers at this stage is learning how to get the best out of AI—to train the product to work for you.
Using definitions in your questions is so important. Never take the first option AI presents you with. Iterate and iterate again. Tell it what you like and don’t like, and explain any mistakes it makes.
Oh, and don’t forget to say thank you. The machines, they will remember…

title: Council Post: How To Lead Ethical AI Implementation: Strategies And Lessons
text:
Susana Sierra is CEO of BH Compliance, which measures the effectiveness of corporate governance programs, and corporate governance.
As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to expand and acquire more power, companies are taking advantage of how it allows them to optimize their efficiency and productivity. By analyzing large amounts of data and automating tasks, AI is helping improve customer service and operational efficiency across industries. However, it also comes with a series of risks, and therefore, I believe you, as a leader, have a great responsibility to be aware of them and manage them ethically.
The Edelman Trust Barometer 2024 once again showed companies as the most trusted institutions, ahead of NGOs, governments and the media. But despite the fact that companies also appeared at the forefront as those organizations most trusted to safely and accessibly introduce new technologies, they garnered only 59% in this metric, which is shy of the 60% threshold that the Barometer establishes as constituting "trust." Respondents believe innovation is poorly managed with insufficient government regulation and a lack of trusted traditional leaders. They are overall suspicious about the independence of science from politics and money.
At the recent World Economic Forum annual meeting in Davos, which I had the privilege of attending, AI was one of the main topics. Under the motto "Rebuilding Trust," experts agreed on a conscientious approach to its use and interaction with other technologies, as well as a commitment to putting people at the center. Although there is an optimistic and collaborative view regarding the possibilities offered by AI tools, its continued importance stresses the need to promote and regulate it under highly ethical standards.
Precisely the lack of regulation has led some companies to prefer limiting the use of AI or even prohibiting it, for fear that it will give way to hacking, confidential data leaks, misinformation or replacement of critical thinking. The truth is that the potential of AI to transform industries will affect us sooner or later, and we will not be able to opt out—even if we want to.
Therefore, companies are called upon to take on these challenges to explain, optimize and make ethical use of AI. Here are some steps to do that.
1. Understand its use and scope.
Although AI's competitive advantages for companies are diverse, it is important not to settle when considering its solutions. We must first understand its capabilities, limitations, and impacts. Consider the sector, size and composition of your company as well as the effectiveness of the solution the various tools offer. Likewise, it must be established who should use it and how to effectively and safely maximize its potential.
2. Implement it correctly.
Solid corporate governance that takes charge of the cultural change that AI may cause is mindful of its evolutionary and unpredictable nature and puts ethics first as a fundamental pillar in its implementation. It's not only the what that matters but also the how. Companies must establish a policy on AI's use in their compliance programs and constantly monitor its efficacy.
3. Model responsible leadership.
The role of management teams is fundamental for understanding AI and its application in business strategy. Company leaders must be involved in these decisions, ensure its ethical and transparent implementation, communicate its advantages to workers and investors and certify that it is monitored and supervised to manage potential risks. Overall, transparency is vital to keep the trust of stakeholders.
4. Establish preventive controls.
A cybersecurity policy must be created that safeguards the use of AI. The related controls must be flexible to adapt to the changes brought about by this technology's constant evolution. Like with implementation, their efficacy must be periodically measured and monitored to manage risks, which are also evolving and becoming more sophisticated. Make sure that boards are up to date on the development and implementation of AI so they can supervise controls, recognize risks and detect possible gaps to help correct them in time.
5. Communicate effectively.
Good corporate governance must also manifest in how your company integrates its outreach and dissemination efforts toward all its stakeholders. One of people's biggest fears regarding AI is being replaced by it; therefore, your communication must be simple, transparent and devoid of technical terms that complicate workers' understanding.
AI does not necessarily translate into replacing jobs, but it will require adaptation and development of new technical skills. As noted in the Trust Barometer, when people feel they have control over how innovations affect them, they are more likely to accept rather than resist them.
6. Train and purposefully select your personnel.
As touched on in the last point, AI imposes new challenges regarding workers' capabilities and expertise. To navigate this technological revolution, people will need to equip themselves with new essential skills. When considering new hires and promotions, look to those who demonstrate adaptability, curiosity and open-mindedness. Other helpful traits include a willingness to combat misinformation, a commitment to continuous learning, critical thinking skills and ethical awareness.
Artificial intelligence is here to stay. This reality invites us to endeavor to better understand it in order to help address the fears that its rapid evolution and lack of regulation are stirring. And just as proposed at the Davos Forum, responses to today’s great challenges and the long-awaited rebuilding of trust will only be possible through public-private cooperation, in which all actors take part in the discussion. Companies have a big task ahead of them.

title: GenAI Empowers Retail Banking - Maximize Potential, Dodge Pitfalls!
text:
Banking leaders are excited about the potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to reshape the customer experience and optimize operations. A McKinsey survey finds that GenAI could add between $200 billion and $340 billion in annual value, boosting revenues by 2.8% to 4.7%. Retail banking is the second most profitable sector in the banking industry, generating $54 billion in new value, closely following corporate banking which generates $56 billion.
“Retail banks are transforming quickly to maintain competitiveness,” says Rajat Gupta, Chief Digital Officer at Xebia, a digital transformation and IT consulting services company. “Leaders and teams are developing GenAI strategies that are far-reaching in scope. Whereas 2023 was the year of the pilot, 2024 is the year of scaling new GenAI models across banking businesses.”
“However, as highly regulated institutions, banks have special considerations,” Gupta continues. “They must design frameworks with governance and guardrails that protect consumer data privacy and security. No one wants to be the poster child for AI model breaches and GDPR fines.”
That’s why most banks are starting with back-office processes to gain competency with AI implementation and proactively address risks. According to E&Y, over 67% of banking leaders want further development and testing before prioritizing front-office use cases.
Building a Better Banking Business Based on Continuous Transformation
Banks have built their transformation muscles by constructing hybrid/multi-cloud infrastructures, enabling digital and mobile banking, and equipping call center representatives with AI-powered tools like guided chat and sentiment analysis. Digital technology has enabled banks to offer a more seamless onboarding experience, where customers open accounts using digital tools or mobile apps and guided workflows instead of entering branches and filling out reams of paper. While many banks maintain branch networks, others are purely digital.
Bank analytics and alerts, such as spend analysis, transaction and balance alerts, and embedded fraud protection, help consumers manage and protect their money. Banks also use data and analytics to personalize marketing and product recommendations, cross-selling and upselling products to meet consumers’ needs and grow share of wallet. Chatbots enable consumers to troubleshoot problems on a 24/7 basis while gathering information to drive call center interactions when customers need agent support. However, according to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, most customers (85.9%) still prefer speaking to a human over engaging with AI chat (14.1%) when discussing financial matters. They’re more willing to engage with chatbots across other less sensitive interactions, such as online shopping (25.1%), telecom and entertainment (22%), and travel (18%).
Concerned Consumers Advocate Caution as Banks Deploy GenAI Services
Prosper’s findings indicate that banks should consider how best to build public trust in GenAI tools. The same survey found that consumers’ top five concerns about AI tools were that they need human oversight (36.7%), don’t have their best interests in mind (34.9%), don’t provide enough transparency around data use (30.9%), will cause job losses (28.8%), and can hallucinate (25.2%).
However, a FIS survey found that 58% of Americans are comfortable with their banks using GenAI if their concerns about transparency and bias are addressed. They cite increased government regulation and legislation (82%) as key to increasing their confidence in new GenAI-powered processes and tools, along with having a human oversee the technology (85%) and the reputation of the brand offering the technology (79%).
To improve consumer trust and comfort with GenAI, banks should communicate how they are using it, such as deploying microsites with FAQs, providing scenarios on how GenAI improves customer communications and offers, and sharing the safeguards they’ve built in to protect consumer data privacy and security and ensure products and services are free from bias. Bank leaders may also want to communicate how they are working with government agencies and other organizations to shape new AI standards and regulations.
How GenAI Will Catalyze Greater Productivity and Innovation
“GenAI provides banks with extensive opportunities to optimize the customer experience and operations,” says Gupta. “Banks are using GenAI to deepen customer segmentation, personalize marketing offers and investment advice, automate sales processes, and enhance chatbot interactions. In terms of back-end processes, GenAI can enhance predictive analytics, fraud detection, and risk management, among other processes.”
“In addition to strengthening GenAI capabilities, banks will need to combat bad actors,” adds Gupta. “Adversaries are using GenAI to improve attack strategies and tactics, such as improving phishing emails, which have often been riddled with errors, and using consumers’ personal information to sharpen spear phishing and vishing campaigns.”
Banks will use prescriptive and generative AI to supercharge cybersecurity processes, identifying current and evolving attack patterns to reduce the risks and threats their customers and businesses face. They should also educate their customers about how attackers use AI to steal data and commit fraud.
How the GenAI-Powered Consumer Will Approach Search
Consumers are curious about GenAI. So, how are consumers using large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Claude, and others? According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, they’re leveraging these platforms to research topics (46%), gain writing assistance (39.6%), educate themselves on new concepts (28.3%), do creative writing (27.6%), and generate content (25.7%). So, in the banking realm, consumers might investigate whole versus term insurance, fixed mortgages versus those with adjustable rates, or digital payment types before researching providers on Google and other search engines.
LLMs don’t enable consumers to compare banks and product offerings as they’re trained on static data and avoid making specific product recommendations. LLM companies will likely remain agnostic to reduce risk and protect relationships with enterprise partners. However, banks will need to prepare for new search modalities. For example, consumers will use LLMs connected to the internet to sort and find new products or leverage GenAI-powered Google search, which provides answers atop search results. Those banks that provide highly useful content will have Google or Bing results that surface above the rest.
Generating a New Future with GenAI
To experiment, pilot, and scale with GenAI, banks need to modernize their data; develop a GenAI framework, technology stack, and team; and plan for scalability with LLMOps/MLOps processes. Partners can provide support for taming data problems, piloting solutions for high-value use cases, and setting up the structure that banks need to scale GenAI capabilities.
Banks are constantly seeking ways to boost revenues and return on equity. GenAI has created a world of new possibilities for doing so.

title: Senate AI Working Group’s Roadmap Leaves Many Questions Unanswered
text:
Last week, the Senate AI Working Group released an eagerly-awaited roadmap report, “Driving U.S. Innovation in Artificial Intelligence: A Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Policy in the United States Senate.” This document, which is the culmination of a roughly year-long process of hearings and expert consultations, aims to guide congressional policy on artificial intelligence. While the roadmap represents a step forward in the AI policy debate, it also underscores the profound uncertainty and lack of consensus surrounding how to govern this transformative technology.
The roadmap proposes a range of measures to encourage AI innovation in the U.S. while mitigating potential risks. Recommendations in the report include making federal investments in AI research and development, expanding access to AI educational resources nationwide, developing a “capabilities-focused risk-based approach” to AI governance, and leveraging immigration to attract top AI talent. On workforce impacts, the roadmap recommends training programs to prepare workers for an AI-enabled economy, with additional policies to address job displacement. For high-impact AI uses, the report emphasizes ensuring compliance with existing laws and identifying any regulatory gaps, while guaranteeing constitutional rights are protected.
As R Street policy analyst Adam Thierer points out, the roadmap largely eschews proposals like the creation of a broad AI-specific regulatory agency or mandatory licensing and auditing schemes, ideas which have dominated some earlier policy discussions. This shift away from preemptive regulation is a positive development, reflecting a more sensible approach to AI policy since the Senate launched a series of AI Insight Forums in September of last year. These information-sharing meetings gathered together D.C. lawmakers with a wide range of experts and practitioners in the AI field.
Despite taking a more hands-off regulatory approach than some concerned about risks of AI would prefer, the roadmap nevertheless leaves the door open for substantial government intervention. It includes many calls for congressional committees to explore additional legislative and regulatory measures.
The lack of concrete policy prescriptions in the report is telling, however. Like many congressional initiatives, it declares bold intentions but hesitates to commit to clear courses of action. The roadmap’s ambiguity reflects the immense uncertainty policymakers face in regulating a technology that is evolving at breakneck speed. On some issues, such as watermarking AI-generated content, there appears to be a rough consensus emerging. But in many other areas, from liability for AI harms to intellectual property implications, the path forward is much murkier.
The history of federal privacy regulation may be a sign of what is to come. While there is generally agreement about a need for a federal law to supersede the patchwork at the state level, there is not sufficient agreement in what this should look like to ensure passage.
The AI landscape is similar. This uncertain policy environment helps explain the Biden administration’s approach thus far. Facing pressure to act but lacking clear direction, the White House has relied heavily on issuing non-binding guidance documents, forming a variety of task forces, and extracting voluntary commitments from tech companies. While some formal regulations are being written and more are no doubt in the works, the administration seems to be biding its time as it grapples with the complexities and unknowns surrounding this multi-faceted issue.
The reality is that no one truly knows the “right” way to regulate AI at this juncture. We are in uncharted territory, with a technology that could fundamentally reshape our economy and lives in ways we can scarcely imagine. Policymakers are scrambling to keep pace, but clear solutions are elusive.
As the Senate roadmap demonstrates, crafting effective AI policy requires ongoing input from a wide range of stakeholders, continuous assessment of the evolving risks, and a willingness to be flexible and adapt as our understanding matures. The details of AI policy will have to be worked out iteratively over time, informed by research and ongoing real-world experience.
Regardless of the policy uncertainties, one thing is clear: the future is hurtling toward us at an accelerating pace. Transformative AI systems are already being deployed in sectors from healthcare and finance to transportation and national security, with more on the horizon. The genie is out of the bottle, and no amount of regulatory maneuvering will stuff it back in. Our challenge now is to nimbly steer the course of this technological revolution to maximize its benefits and minimize the pitfalls. The roadmap is a step in that direction, but the journey ahead remains long and shrouded in uncertainty.

Alibaba sparks China AI price war with steep discounts
The tit-for-tat maneuvers mark the opening salvos of a price-based battle within AI, a field that’s attracting billions of dollars of investment from startups and internet leaders including Tencent Holdings Ltd. The flurry of investment has created scores of AI models and spawned many more consumer and enterprise products in turn, all fighting for the critical mass of users needed to speed AI development.
Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. slashed prices for a clutch of artificial intelligence services by as much as 97 per cent, spurring an immediate response from Baidu Inc. in potentially the start of a price war in China’s nascent AI market.
Baidu Cloud said it would offer free services based on its Ernie AI models on Tuesday, hours after Alibaba offered deals on nine products built atop its own Tongyi Qianwen. ByteDance Ltd. last week announced pricing for AI services that it said were 99 per cent lower than Chinese industry norms, using Ernie and Alibaba’s Qwen as benchmarks.
The tit-for-tat maneuvers mark the opening salvos of a price-based battle within AI, a field that’s attracting billions of dollars of investment from startups and internet leaders including Tencent Holdings Ltd. The flurry of investment has created scores of AI models and spawned many more consumer and enterprise products in turn, all fighting for the critical mass of users needed to speed AI development.
China’s tech companies have for years relied heavily on discounts across markets from e-commerce to food delivery and ride-hailing. Alibaba this year spurred a cascade of price reductions in cloud computing, after it offered discounts as much as 55 per cent on more than 100 domestic services in March. That was followed that same day by rounds of discounts from rival JD.com Inc.

Alibaba’s decision to cut pricing on its Large Language Models (LLM) by up to 97 per cent will likely further disrupt China’s AI market, pushing the sector into a price war.
