title: Council Post: How To Navigate AI-Driven Layoffs Without Losing Employee Trust
text:
As businesses increasingly embrace artificial intelligence in their operations, thousands of workers have already lost their jobs, with AI-driven layoffs having continued month after month so far this year. With more of the same on the horizon, employers need to proactively ensure their processes, policies and communications create understanding among the employees who remain with their organizations, rather than confusion and fear.
Below, 14 Forbes Coaches Council members explore what leaders navigating AI-driven layoffs can do to create clarity and transparency and maintain trust with remaining team members.
1. Take Care Of Displaced Employees
Taking care of employees on their way out the door is the best way to ease tension for those still inside the house. A cold, heartless layoff will do nothing but add to the tension. Give the displaced employees the resources and the support they need to set their job search up for success, and internal employees will take notice of that. - Franklin Buchanan, Post Up Careers
2. Offer Job Transition Assistance And Upskilling Initiatives
To proactively manage AI-driven layoffs and minimize confusion and fear, employers should be transparent about the AI, the rationale and the potential job impacts. Provide comprehensive support for laid-off workers, including job transition assistance. For remaining staff, reiterate the company’s vision and direction and how their roles and skills remain valuable in the AI era. Invest in reskilling and upskilling initiatives. - Richard Chiumento, The Rialto Consultancy
3. Be Transparent Throughout The Process
It’s important to share the reasons for the layoffs and the remaining team’s importance in providing clients with competitive value. Reinforce values and respect for all team members, and do layoffs all at once, not in dribs and drabs. Folks are smart. Most will wonder why it took you so long. Be candid and honest, and genuinely show you care about your team and the welfare of their company. - Jay McDonald, Middleton McDonald Group, Inc.
4. Leave Final Personnel Decisions To Humans
AI is a great assistant, but it’s terrible at autonomous support. When it comes to personnel decisions and activities, AI should be in a “trust but verify” mode, and it should never make the final personnel decisions regarding hiring or firing. Periodically, verify AI activities and decisions, and embed key process confirmation steps in your processes so that you keep a pulse on what’s happening. - John Knotts, Crosscutter Enterprises
Forbes Coaches Council is an invitation-only community for leading business and career coaches. Do I qualify?
5. Clearly Explain Your Reasoning
Employers should focus on transparency, open communication and educating employees about the company’s direction. Transparently explaining the reasons and criteria for layoffs reassures employees about the fairness of the process. Regular communication helps alleviate fears and quash rumors. Educating the workforce about the organization’s future plans and their role in it can inspire confidence. - Farshad Asl, Top Leaders, Inc.
6. Define How AI Is Used In Your Business
Adapt the organization’s social contract by clearly stating that AI is a profound support tool for employees to improve their roles and performance. Provide tools for employees to experiment with and progressively use AI more in their daily work. This will rapidly move the organization forward without significant labor loss. - Gideon Malherbe, Virtual Consulting
7. Follow Established Internal Processes
Unfortunately, all organizations should always have an up-to-date layoff process in place—and hope that they never need to use it. It should provide a clearly defined process for handling communications (with impacted individuals as well as the larger organization), benefits, internal job placement and outplacement, FAQs and so on. Every effort should be made to do one layoff and avoid multiple small layoffs. - Kathy Bernhard, KFB Leadership Solutions
8. Anticipate Your Team’s Emotional Needs
When coaching leaders in this area, a focus on increasing their ability to communicate effectively with their teams is essential. In situations where emotions can run high, such as during layoffs, it is important to be open about what is occurring as well as the reasoning behind it to reduce confusion. Build credibility with your remaining employees by being objective and aware of the emotions that surface. - Bryan Powell, Executive Coaching Space
9. Emphasize Employee Growth Opportunities
Roles may shift, but epic team members are always valuable to the team. Create opportunities for personal growth and professional training that emphasizes agility and confidence in the midst of change. Skills can be taught much more easily than passion or purpose, so be sure to communicate to team members that they are part of the company’s future vision even when roles change. - Meridith Alexander, G.R.I.T. Mindset Academy
10. Share A Vision Of The Future
For any kind of downsizing, whether it’s driven by AI, industry downturns or other reasons, communications need to center around what the organization is going to look like in the future and how the remaining employees are going to play a part in that future. There is a reason why the workers who remain still do—and it is important for them to know that. - Basav Ray Chaudhuri, Coach with Basav
11. Help Employees Learn How To Adapt
The only competence that is pivotal in an AI-driven world is learning, and that’s why leaders should focus on helping people learn how to quickly adapt to unexpected changes, welcoming them with joy as signs of new transformation. The next step is to learn new skills to capitalize on new opportunities. Losing a job can be a gift when people are ready to seize the opportunities it presents. - Dominik Szot, MIA
12. Make A Plan To Manage Upcoming Changes
In my experience, many organizations have “dropped the ball” with their approach to recent layoffs. This is the time to pick up the ball and make a plan to manage the change that lies ahead. Begin by educating all employees on the impact of AI on their work. Then create a change management plan that includes transparent communications, redeployment strategies and frequent updates on impact timing. - Jill Helmer, Jill Helmer Consulting
13. Frame AI Adoption As A Transition
Frame AI adoption with clear communication and a sense of “change,” not “ending.” AI is not ending anything; it is changing the way we produce, work and live. The same fear arose when computers were invented—and today, we know that our daily lives just changed, and nobody lost anything. What can each and every person change in their own life to thrive and transform into something new? - David Kubes, Access Consciousness Leadership
14. Take A Multi-Pronged Approach
Understand that a multi-pronged approach is required, even at a multi-stakeholder level. Showing insensitivity in the process will cripple a company’s reputation, as proven by recent high-profile restructurings. Mechanize AI to help create scenarios and actions across the ecosystem to manage both the layoff and post-layoff process. Equip and empower your people to enable that. AI is just a tool. - Arthi Rabikrisson, Prerna Advisory

title: Council Post: Three Questions Every Leader Needs To Ask About AI Cybersecurity
text:
Kasada CTO, stopping bot attacks that others can't stop with novel mitigation techniques that beat cybercriminals at their own game.
As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies evolve, they continue to reshape the cybersecurity landscape—both as a formidable defense mechanism and, paradoxically, as a potent tool for threat actors. AI is rapidly lowering the barrier to entry for cybercriminals, providing them with sophisticated means to launch attacks that were once out of reach. Despite the best efforts of generative AI (GenAI) developers to secure technologies with rigorous guardrails, attackers continue to find creative ways to circumvent these protections.
Headlines reveal how attackers harness AI to craft convincing phishing emails or spread disinformation. However, the misuse of AI runs deeper, with bad actors deploying AI to undermine security systems. This technological double-edged sword isn’t just a concern for cybersecurity teams but also has wide-ranging implications for business leaders.
That’s because AI deployments also carry significant economic risks. For instance, through techniques such as prompt injection, attackers can manipulate AI applications to elicit unintended responses, thereby extracting sensitive information and inadvertently shifting computational costs to the victim. Similarly, denial of wallet (DoW) attacks inflate operational costs by overwhelming AI systems with automated requests, causing financial harm and operational disruption. Both of these methods illustrate how AI systems can be exploited to rapidly amplify costs for businesses, turning technology investments into liabilities.
Moreover, the inherent complexity and continuous evolution of large language models (LLMs) and GenAI systems contribute to their vulnerability. The opaque nature of these systems often leaves even their developers in the dark about potential weaknesses, thereby complicating the defense against such novel attacks. As these models are being continuously updated to enhance their capabilities, new vulnerabilities can quietly emerge, further challenging security teams to keep pace.
How Threat Actors Exploit AI
Threat actors are increasingly finding creative ways to use AI to evolve their tactics and unearth new vulnerabilities. While their tactics vary widely, most can be categorized into three principal methods, each of which demonstrates the dual-use nature of these technologies.
1. Adversarial Inputs: One of the most direct ways threat actors are using AI today involves creating adversarial inputs that manipulate how AI systems classify data by reverse-engineering the system’s classification mechanisms. For instance, an attacker might craft specific requests that are then submitted to an AI system responsible for classifying data. By tweaking the data submitted, attackers can learn how to manipulate the system from afar. A notable example of this technique is the "many-shot jail-breaking" of large language models, as discussed in this recent blog post by Anthropic. This method involves overwhelming an AI with a high volume of queries to trick it into providing a response it typically wouldn’t, thus bypassing the intended operational parameters.
2. Data Poisoning: Data poisoning aims to corrupt the underlying model of a security system by blurring the line between legitimate and malicious classifications. By flooding the system with misleading data from various sources, attackers aim to retrain the AI’s perception of normalcy. For example, an attacker might repeatedly send a malicious payload from numerous points over an extended period of time, with the goal of slowly nudging the classification from malicious to benign. By exploiting the learning capabilities of an AI system, this method seeks to turn a strength—adaptability and learning from new information—into a vulnerability.
3. Black Box Probing: The third significant method is black box probing, which combines elements of adversarial inputs and data poisoning. This technique involves sending a myriad of queries to a system to understand and eventually replicate the model’s decision-making process. This method is often seen in attempts to break CAPTCHA systems, where attackers progressively adapt to the increasing complexity of CAPTCHAs driven by advanced AI models. By reverse engineering these models, attackers can create algorithms that bypass CAPTCHA with high efficiency, demonstrating a deep understanding of AI behavior.
Three Questions To Ask Of Your AI Security
For business leaders, understanding the nuances and potential vulnerabilities of AI-powered tools must be a priority, particularly in light of economic exploitation risks. As AI becomes further enmeshed within security frameworks, the potential for these kinds of attacks only increases. To get a more complete picture of these risks, consider the following three questions.
1. How does AI enhance our visibility into the threat landscape? Enhanced visibility into the threat landscape is a critical advantage of using AI in cybersecurity. Leaders should evaluate whether AI tools are providing a clearer demarcation between benign and malicious activities—whether they allow for a deeper analysis of behavioral patterns around these boundaries. The ability to detect subtle anomalies or trends can significantly bolster a company's defensive posture, making it an essential consideration for integrating AI effectively.
2. What strategic advantages does AI bring to our cybersecurity efforts? It’s vital to assess the efficiency gains from deploying AI within your security operations. Leaders should ask how these technologies are enhancing the capabilities of their security teams and whether they are translating into more effective risk mitigation. This includes examining both direct benefits from in-house AI applications and those derived from partnerships with AI-equipped vendors. The goal is to ensure that the implementation of AI is not just a technological upgrade but a strategic enhancement that fortifies the organization's overall security framework.
3. How reliable are the AI capabilities of our security partners? Choosing the right partners is pivotal in leveraging external AI capabilities. Business leaders need to carefully evaluate how their security partners utilize AI in service delivery. For example, if a partner is using AI to analyze network traffic patterns to predict and preempt potential breaches, you should work to understand the data-driven methodologies behind these capabilities. It's crucial for leaders to be informed and critical about the AI tools their partners use, ensuring these technologies align with their own data security needs and standards.
By addressing these questions, business leaders can provide a measure of assurance that their investment in AI-driven cybersecurity is not just about adopting new technology but also about making a strategic, informed decision that enhances their resilience against both conventional and next-wave AI-driven threats.

title: Generative AI: Deal Me In
text:
Everyone knows the cautionary tale of Blockbuster Video. The shorthand version is that the video-rental chain, which operated thousands of stores and reported revenues of $6 billion in 2004, had to declare bankruptcy just six years later because it disregarded the threat of online streaming services. But there’s more to the story. Many may have forgotten that co-founders of a, now well-known, streaming giant tried to sell their, at the time, fledgling online startup to Blockbuster in 2000 for a mere $50 million.
This recollection of the missed Blockbuster opportunity came to me while speaking with business leaders about, of all things, generative AI.
Expanding the generative AI conversation
I’ve spent a lot of time over the past year talking to executives about potential uses of generative AI in their businesses. I’m lucky in that regard since it’s a topic I find equal parts fascinating as well as game changing.
Fortunately, business leaders do too. Our research shows that nearly all of them (85%) are investing in the technology. And they’re doing so quickly. Half of them plan on having their capabilities fully scaled in the next six to 12 months. They’re moving fast because they've seen the speed with which generative AI can transform any and all areas of an organization. And they’ve seen the value that can be captured by peers who quickly experiment and move to scaling generative AI as a driver of productivity across their organizations. The race is on.
Zeroing in on M&A
Many of my recent conversations with CEOs have been focused on the use of generative AI in the M&A function. That’s not surprising, given that 70% of M&A decisionmakers expect that generative AI can help boost expected returns on their transactions. Which brings us back to the Blockbuster story.
Of course, we will never know. But we can imagine that Blockbuster might have used generative AI to assess the feasibility of the acquisition.
That’s how more and more M&A practitioners are using it today. Accenture
The untapped post-deal opportunity
Dealmakers also recognize that there is value to be had from generative AI in the post-deal world – but they aren’t making the most of the opportunity before them yet. Our research shows that 64% of M&A executives expect generative AI to revolutionize M&A deal processes. Yet only one-third (35%) say they are investing heavily in the technology for M&A purposes.
This is a costly oversight that would limit the likelihood of a successful integration.
Generative AI can, for example, standardize a host of post-deal tasks, streamline the design of transition service agreements (TSAs), and facilitate the integration of systems and infrastructures. It can also bring more creativity to the mix by rendering new operating models and organizational structures while aiding post-merger performance assessments, synergy capture acceleration and incremental opportunity identification. Together, these post-deal applications of generative AI present a huge— and relatively untapped—opportunity.
Seizing the end-to-end opportunity
Generative AI’s contribution to M&A transaction value is substantial—especially when dealmakers lead with value and use the technology to transform pre- and post-deal activities. I’d go so far as to say that the use of generative AI across the M&A lifecycle will be a key determinant of the overall success (or failure) of deals in the future. But I believe that it will take three key points:
The first, as noted, involves identifying opportunities across the M&A lifecycle. But that must be followed with a concerted effort to reinvent talent and ways of working to make the best use of generative AI tools and insights. Dealmakers who can gather intelligence and insights faster—and free up enough time along the way to focus on making strategic design decisions—will win in the end.
Second is that M&A leaders also need to understand that a strong digital core is essential for generative AI to effectively contribute to their activities. This infrastructure must support seamless data flow and collaboration across different parts of the organization, while ensuring data security and ethical usage—key aspects of "Responsible AI."
Finally, M&A leaders who want to get the most from their investments need to adopt a mindset of continuous reinvention. The use of generative AI across the M&A lifecycle is steadily accelerating. So is the pace of change dealmakers are encountering. That means any AI-enabled M&A reinvention strategy must be dynamic. It must be designed to evolve over time. It must help prepare practitioners for what’s next.
Deal me in
It’s an exciting time for many, and it should equally be for dealmakers. They now have a technology that can help them optimize every step of a merger or acquisition—from target identification all the way to final, post-integration execution and value capture. Of course, generative AI alone won’t ensure a deal’s success. But it can significantly improve the likelihood that we will be talking about other blockbuster deals in the future. The good kind. The kind other leaders want to emulate.
